lessons.unit: R13-R16: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: proportional equations, rates and growth
lessons.title: Proportional equations: x², 1/x and beyond
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a quantity change when the thing it depends on is squared?
objectives: Write proportionality statements as equations with a constant k
Solve problems with y ∝ x², y ∝ x³, y ∝ √x, y ∝ 1/x and y ∝ 1/x²
Describe how changing one variable changes another
successCriteria: All: write and use y = kx or y = k/x
Most: write and use equations involving squares and square roots
Some: find a percentage change in y from a percentage change in x
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: inverse square law of light and gravity
lessons.smsc: Reflection on signs in creation: patterns in light and sound obey exact mathematical laws.

keywords.def: changes by a constant multiple of
the value k in the equation
y = k/x: as x increases, y decreases

starter: Bismillah. y = 4x. Find y when x = 7.
Write 'y is inversely proportional to x' as an equation with k.

teach.heading: From words to equations
teach.note: Common thread: always replace ∝ by = k × the expression. Then use a pair of values to find k, rewrite the formula with k, and only then answer the question.

teach.heading: y proportional to x squared

model.problem: y is directly proportional to the square of x. y = 45 when x = 3. Find y when x = 7 and x when y = 20.
steps: y = kx² so 45 = k × 9 and k = 5

teach.note: Use the formula y = 5x². Discuss: if x doubles then y goes up by a factor of 4. Check the sign of x with the context.

teach.heading: Inverse square

model.problem: The light intensity I from a lamp is inversely proportional to the square of the distance d from it. I = 90 when d = 2 m. Find I when d = 6 m and d when I = 40.
steps: I = k/d² so 90 = k/4 and k = 360

teach.note: Show how three times as far gives a ninth of the brightness. The same pattern governs gravity (Newton's law) which supports the idea that the universe follows precise laws.

teach.heading: Hinge: the equation

check.q: 'y is inversely proportional to the square of x' is written:
check.why: Inverse means divide: y = k/x². y = kx² is direct; y = k/x is inverse proportion (not squared).

teach.note: Whiteboards. Then give the numbers: y = 4 when x = 3: k = 36.

teach.heading: Percentage change

model.problem: y is inversely proportional to x². x increases by 20%. Find the percentage change in y.

teach.note: Higher style: do not choose numbers; use the multiplier. Alternatively test with x = 10 and k = 100. ANSWERS: practice: 245; y = 36/x² so 1 and x = 2; 10; k = 2 so 250. exit: 45; 15. core: k = 2, x = 6; k = 24, y = 4; k = 2, T = 6. extend: k = 14/900, d ≈ 38.9 m; doubling v multiplies d by 4. stretch: 30.6% decrease. homework: P = 300/V and P = 60 kPa.

practice: y ∝ x². y = 45 when x = 3. Find y when x = 7.
y ∝ 1/x². y = 4 when x = 3. Find y when x = 6 and x when y = 9.
I is inversely proportional to d². I = 90 when d = 2. Find I when d = 6.
y is proportional to the cube of x. y = 54 when x = 3. Find y when x = 5.
independent: Core: a) y ∝ x², y = 50 when x = 5: find x when y = 72. b) y ∝ 1/x, y = 3 when x = 8: find y when x = 6. c) T ∝ √L, T = 3 when L = 2.25: find T when L = 9.
Extend: The braking distance d metres is proportional to the square of the speed v mph. d = 14 when v = 30. Find d when v = 50 to 3 s.f. How does d change if v doubles?
Stretch: y is inversely proportional to the square of x. x increases by 20%. Find the percentage change in y.
exit: y ∝ x². y = 20 when x = 2. Find y when x = 3.
y ∝ 1/x. y = 12 when x = 5. Find y when x = 4.
Big question: How does a quantity change when the thing it depends on is squared?
lessons.homework: Pressure P kPa is inversely proportional to volume V litres. P = 150 when V = 2. Find P when V = 5, and write the equation.
lessons.send: SEND: use a four-step frame (write ∝, replace by = k, find k, answer) for every question. EAL: 'directly', 'inversely', 'square of'. Stretch: if y ∝ x² and x ∝ 1/z then y ∝ 1/z². Higher-only: constructing equations with squares, cubes, roots and inverse squares (R13). Foundation: recognising inverse proportion.

lessons.unit: R13-R16: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: proportional equations, rates and growth
lessons.title: Gradients as rates of change; graphs of proportion
lessons.bigQuestion: What does the steepness of a graph tell us?
objectives: Interpret the gradient of a straight-line graph as a rate of change
Use units to describe the rate
Recognise graphs of direct and inverse proportion
successCriteria: All: find a gradient and interpret it as a rate in context
Most: interpret the intercept and the gradient in a linear model
Some: recognise and sketch graphs of y = kx, y = k/x and y = kx²
lessons.crossCurricular: Science and finance: speed-time and cost graphs
lessons.smsc: Honesty with numbers: reading a graph accurately, without exaggerating a trend.

keywords.def: change in y divided by change in x
how fast one quantity changes with respect to another
where a graph crosses the y-axis

starter: Find the gradient of the line through (1, 3) and (5, 11).
Find y when x = 4 in y = 2x + 3.
Describe the shape of the graph of y = 1/x.

teach.heading: Gradient means 'per'
bullets: Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x
The units are y-units per x-unit
Distance-time graph: gradient = speed
Speed-time graph: gradient = acceleration
teach.note: Show the units idea: if the vertical axis is km and the horizontal is hours, the gradient is km per hour. Ask what a horizontal line on a distance-time graph means (not moving).

teach.heading: Interpreting a graph

model.problem: A taxi charges £4 plus £2.50 per mile: C = 4 + 2.5m. What do the gradient and the intercept mean?
model.answer: Gradient £2.50 per mile; intercept £4 fixed charge

teach.note: Not proportional because the line does not go through the origin. Compare with a proportional model C = 2.5m.

teach.heading: Hinge: speed

check.q: A distance-time graph is a straight line from (0, 0) to (2, 150), with distance in km and time in hours. The speed is:
check.why: Gradient = 150 ÷ 2 = 75 km/h. 150 is the distance; 300 doubles; 1/75 inverts.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask what the gradient would be if the graph was steeper.

teach.heading: Recognising graphs

right.title: Inverse proportion y = k/x
points: Curve in two parts, never touching the axes

teach.note: Draw both quickly. Table check: y = 12/x gives (1, 12), (2, 6), (3, 4), (4, 3), (6, 2), (12, 1): the product is always 12. y = kx² is a U-shaped parabola through the origin.

teach.heading: Speed-time graph

model.problem: A speed-time graph goes in a straight line from (0, 0) to (8, 24), speed in m/s and time in s. Find the acceleration.
steps: Gradient = change in speed ÷ change in time

teach.note: Acceleration is the rate of change of speed. The area under the line is the distance travelled: 1/2 × 8 × 24 = 96 m. ANSWERS: practice: 75 km/h; 0.3 means £0.30 per unit and 12 is the fixed charge; y = 3x straight through origin, y = 12/x two-branch curve, y = x² U-shape; 3 m/s². exit: 3; two branches, never touching the axes. core: gradient 8 litres per minute, V = 8t, V = 96 litres; rate -20% per hour so battery lasts 5 hours; y = 5x only (the line through the origin). stretch: y = 3x + 2 is not direct proportion because it does not pass through the origin. homework: C = 8 + 0.4g, gradient 0.4, intercept 8; not directly proportional.

practice: A distance-time graph goes through (0, 0) and (2, 150). Find the speed.
C = 12 + 0.3u gives the cost in pounds of u units. Interpret the gradient and intercept.
Sketch the graphs of y = 3x, y = 12/x and y = x². State one feature of each.
A speed-time graph goes from (0, 0) to (8, 24). Find the acceleration.
independent: Core: a) The graph of volume V litres against time t minutes passes through (0, 0) and (5, 40). Find the gradient and write V in terms of t. b) Predict V at t = 12.
Extend: A phone battery is 100% at time 0 and 40% after 3 hours. Find the rate of change in % per hour and when it reaches 0, assuming a constant rate.
Stretch: Which of these graphs shows direct proportion: y = 3x + 2, y = 5x, y = 12/x, y = x²? Explain.
exit: Find the gradient between (2, 5) and (8, 23).
Describe the graph of y = 6/x.
Big question: What does the steepness of a graph tell us?
lessons.homework: A mobile plan costs £8 per month plus 40p for each GB of data. Write a formula, state the gradient and the intercept, and say whether the cost is directly proportional to the data used.
lessons.send: SEND: label the axes with units and write 'rise ÷ run' on the graph; use a pre-drawn grid. EAL: 'per', 'rate', 'gradient'. Stretch: interpret a curved distance-time graph (next lesson). Foundation-accessible throughout; the y = kx² sketch is an extension.

lessons.unit: R13-R16: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: proportional equations, rates and growth
lessons.title: Tangents and instantaneous rate of change
lessons.bigQuestion: How fast is something changing at exactly this moment?
objectives: Distinguish average and instantaneous rate of change
Estimate the gradient of a curve at a point by drawing a tangent
Interpret the gradient in context
successCriteria: All: draw a tangent and find its gradient
Most: estimate an instantaneous rate using shrinking intervals
Some: interpret the answer with units in context
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: speed at an instant
lessons.smsc: Patience and accuracy in measurement: small errors in drawing change the answer.

keywords.def: a straight line that touches a curve at one point and has the same direction there
the rate of change at a single moment
a straight line joining two points on a curve

starter: Write 'speed' as a gradient on a distance-time graph.

teach.heading: Shrinking the interval for d = t²
teach.note: Higher only. As the interval shrinks, the chord's gradient approaches 6: that is the speed at t = 3. The tangent at t = 3 has gradient 6 m/s. Pupils can verify the entries with a calculator.
bullets: Shrinking intervals approach the tangent gradient

teach.heading: Drawing a tangent

model.problem: The distance d = t² metres after t seconds. Draw the curve and a tangent at t = 4. Find the speed at t = 4.
steps: Plot the curve; at (4, 16) place a ruler so that it touches the curve and does not cross it
The tangent passes through about (2, 0) and (6, 32)
Speed at t = 4 is about 8 m/s

teach.note: Accept 7 to 9 m/s. Stress the balance of the ruler so the angle between the curve and ruler is equal on both sides. Make the triangle large to reduce error.

teach.heading: Hinge: meaning

check.q: The tangent to a distance-time curve at t = 4 s has gradient 3 m/s. This tells us:
options: the average speed over 4 s is 3 m/s
the speed at the instant t = 4 s is 3 m/s
check.why: A tangent's gradient is the instantaneous rate: the speed at t = 4. The average over 4 s would need a chord from t = 0.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask which line would give the average speed over the first 4 s.

teach.heading: An exponential model

model.problem: A population is P = 100 × 1.2^t after t hours. Estimate the rate of growth at t = 3.
steps: Gradient of a chord centred on t = 3 = (189.3 - 157.7) ÷ 1

teach.note: A symmetric chord gives a very good estimate without drawing. The actual value is 31.5. Compare with the average rate over the whole 3 hours: (172.8 - 100) ÷ 3 = 24.3, which is lower. ANSWERS: practice: 4.1 and 4.01 so 4 m/s; about 6 m/s; the rate of increase of cost is £0.80 per unit at that point; the chord links two points on the curve (average) and the tangent touches at one point (instantaneous). exit: the speed at t = 5 s is 2 m/s; larger triangles reduce the effect of reading errors. core: v(3.01) = 2 × 9.0601 = 18.1202; (18.1202 - 18) ÷ 0.01 = 12.02 ≈ 12 m/s²; the acceleration at t = 3 s. extend: P(2.5) ≈ 157.7 and P(1.5) ≈ 131.5, so the gradient ≈ 26.3 individuals per hour at t = 2. stretch: zero gradient: no change at that instant. homework: speed-time tangent is acceleration; temperature-time tangent is the rate of change of temperature in °C per unit time.

practice: Estimate d = t² gradient at t = 2 by finding the average speed from t = 2 to 2.1 and to 2.01.
Draw d = t² for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6, then a tangent at t = 3 and find its gradient.
A tangent to a cost curve at x = 100 units has gradient 0.8 £ per unit. Interpret.
Explain the difference between the gradient of a chord and of a tangent.
independent: Core: a) v = 2t² (metres per second). Estimate the acceleration at t = 3 by averaging from t = 3 to 3.01. b) Interpret the value.
Extend: The curve P = 100 × 1.2^t: use a chord from t = 1.5 to 2.5 to estimate the rate at t = 2.
Stretch: For a curve with tangent gradient equal to zero at its lowest point, what does this tell us about the rate of change at that point?
exit: The distance travelled is shown by a curve. The tangent at t = 5 s has gradient 2 m/s. State what this means.
Why is it better to use a large triangle when finding a tangent gradient?
Big question: How fast is something changing at exactly this moment?
lessons.homework: Describe in a sentence what a tangent gradient represents in each case: a speed-time curve and a temperature-time curve.
lessons.send: SEND: provide printed curves and a transparent ruler; allow wider tolerance. EAL: 'instantaneous', 'tangent'. Stretch: calculate d = t² average over [t, t + h] algebraically: 2t + h. Higher-only: this whole lesson (R15).

lessons.unit: R13-R16: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: proportional equations, rates and growth
lessons.title: Growth and decay: compound change
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does money (or a population) grow faster each year?
objectives: Use multipliers for repeated percentage change
Solve compound interest, growth and depreciation problems
Use the formula start × multiplier^n
successCriteria: All: calculate compound interest and depreciation with a multiplier
Most: work backwards to find the original amount, and compare simple and compound
Some: solve for the number of periods by trial or in context
lessons.crossCurricular: Economics and science: populations and radioactive decay
lessons.smsc: Islamic finance forbids interest (riba); we study compound growth as a mathematical model that also describes populations, decay and investments in permitted profit-sharing arrangements.

keywords.def: interest added to the amount so that later interest is earned on interest
a fall in value over time
repeated multiplication by the same factor

starter: Find the multiplier for a 3% increase.
Find the multiplier for an 18% decrease.

teach.heading: The compound formula
bullets: Final = start × multiplier^n
Growth of r%: multiplier 1 + r/100
Decay of r%: multiplier 1 - r/100
n is the number of periods (years, hours)
teach.note: Compare with simple interest which adds the same amount each year. Compound: multiply by the same factor each time. Ask pupils which grows faster over 10 years and why.

teach.heading: Compound interest

model.problem: £2000 is invested at 3% compound interest for 5 years. Find the final amount.

teach.note: Round to the nearest penny at the end only. Compare with simple interest: 2000 × 0.03 × 5 = £300 (£2300 total). The difference is the 'interest on interest'.

teach.heading: Depreciation

model.problem: A car worth £15 000 loses 18% of its value each year. Find its value after 3 years.

teach.note: Ask how much it has lost in total: £6729.48, which is 44.9% of the original, not 54%.

teach.heading: Hinge: multiplier

check.q: A value decreases by 8% each year for 3 years. The overall multiplier is:
check.why: Each year multiplies by 0.92, so three years multiplies by 0.92³ ≈ 0.779. 0.76 subtracts 3 × 8%; 1.08³ is growth.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for the overall percentage loss (22.1%).

teach.heading: Working backwards and solving for n

model.problem: After 3 years of 8% growth a population is 12 597.12. Find the original. How many years for £1000 at 6% to exceed £1500?

teach.note: Divide by the multiplier^n to reverse. Trial and improvement on n; it can also be solved with logarithms but that is beyond GCSE. ANSWERS: practice: £2318.55; £8270.52; 986.9 so 987; 7 years. exit: £899.89; 0.9. core: £4967.16; 20 384; simple £150 and compound £157.63. extend: 12 days = 4 half-lives: 5 g; 7 days: 80 × 0.5^(7/3) ≈ 15.9 g. stretch: 0.8⁴ = 0.4096 < 0.5 so 4 years. homework: £6094.97.

practice: Find the value of £2000 invested at 3% compound interest for 5 years.
Find the value of a £15 000 car after 3 years if it loses 18% each year.
A bacteria count of 500 grows by 12% each hour. Find the count after 6 hours.
How many years for £1000 at 6% compound to exceed £1500?
independent: Core: a) £4500 at 2.5% compound for 4 years. b) A town of 25 000 falls by 4% a year: population after 5 years. c) Compare simple and compound interest on £1000 at 5% for 3 years.
Extend: A radioactive sample of 80 g halves every 3 days. Find the mass after 12 days and give a method for 7 days.
Stretch: A car depreciates by 20% each year. After how many whole years is it worth less than half its price?
exit: £800 at 4% compound for 3 years: find the final amount.
A value decreases by 10% a year: write the multiplier.
Big question: Why does money (or a population) grow faster each year?
lessons.homework: Aisha invests £5000 in an account paying 2% compound interest for 10 years. Find the final amount. Write one sentence on why compound growth is faster than simple growth.
lessons.send: SEND: use a table with year-by-year values before the power; allow a calculator. EAL: 'compound', 'depreciation', 'multiplier'. Stretch: find a formula for the n-th year and solve with trial. Higher-only: reverse compound problems and solving for n by trial. Foundation: compound interest with a multiplier.

lessons.unit: R13-R16: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: proportional equations, rates and growth
lessons.title: General iterative processes
lessons.bigQuestion: How can repeating a simple calculation lead us to an exact-enough answer?
objectives: Use an iteration formula with a starting value
Use iteration to solve an equation to a given accuracy
Interpret iterative sequences in context
successCriteria: All: generate terms of a sequence from x(n+1) = f(x(n))
Most: use iteration to find a root to a given accuracy
Some: model a changing quantity with an iterative process
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: algorithms and loops
lessons.smsc: The idea of ihsan: refining step by step until the result is excellent.

keywords.def: repeating a process, using each output as the next input
the first value x₀ of the sequence
a solution of an equation f(x) = 0

starter: Find f(0) and f(1) when f(x) = x³ - 5x + 1.
Use the Ans button: type 2, then work out Ans × 3 - 1 twice.

teach.heading: An iteration formula
bullets: x₍ₙ₊₁₎ = f(xₙ): each term uses the one before
Start with x₀ then calculate x₁, x₂ ...
If terms settle to a value, that is the solution
Use the Ans key to repeat quickly
teach.note: Show the Ans key sequence on a scientific calculator: enter the starting value, press =, then type the formula with Ans in place of x. Stress writing at least 4 decimal places until the digits settle.

teach.heading: Solving an equation by iteration

model.problem: Show that x³ - 5x + 1 = 0 has a root between 0 and 1. Use x₍ₙ₊₁₎ = (xₙ³ + 1)/5 with x₀ = 0 to find the root to 3 d.p.
steps: f(0) = 1 and f(1) = -3: sign change so a root lies between 0 and 1

teach.note: Rearrangement: 5x = x³ + 1 gives the formula. Check by substituting 0.2016 into the original: 0.00819 - 1.008 + 1 = 0.0002 ≈ 0. Explain that the sign change shows a root, the iteration finds it.

teach.heading: Hinge: using the formula

check.q: x₍ₙ₊₁₎ = (xₙ³ + 1)/5 and x₁ = 0.2. The value of x₂ is:
check.why: x₂ = (0.2³ + 1)/5 = 1.008/5 = 0.2016. 0.208 uses 0.2² or rounds; 1.2 forgets the divide by 5.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Show on the calculator with Ans.

teach.heading: A context

model.problem: A loan balance is Bₙ₊₁ = 1.03 Bₙ - 200, starting at B₀ = 5000 (pounds, after each year's interest and payment). Find B₁, B₂ and B₃.

teach.note: Interpret: 3% growth then a £200 payment each year. Ask what would happen if the payment were £150 (the balance rises). Links to R16 growth.

teach.heading: Stopping too early

misconception.wrong: The first two terms agree to 2 d.p. so the root is 0.20
misconception.right: Keep going until the digits agree to the accuracy asked: here 0.2016 and 0.2016 agree to 4 d.p.

teach.note: Say clearly: to give a root to 3 d.p. you need two consecutive terms that round to the same 3 d.p. value. ANSWERS: practice: 5, 14, 41; x₃ ≈ 0.2016; B₁ = 5940, B₂ = 5877.60, B₃ = 5812.70; f(2) = -1, f(3) = 13 so sign change. exit: x₁ = 3, x₂ = 7, x₃ = 15; f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs so the continuous graph crosses the x-axis. core: x₁ = ∛9 ≈ 2.080, x₂ ≈ 2.1105, x₃ ≈ 2.122 (the terms continue to settle near 2.128). extend: Tₙ₊₁ = 0.9Tₙ + 80, T₀ = 1000: 980, 962, 945.8. stretch: stop when two consecutive terms agree to the required accuracy after rounding. homework: Pₙ₊₁ = 1.05Pₙ - 20: P₁ = 400, P₂ = 400, a stable value: 1.05 × 400 - 20 = 400.

practice: x₍ₙ₊₁₎ = 3xₙ - 1, x₀ = 2: find x₁, x₂, x₃.
Use x₍ₙ₊₁₎ = (xₙ³ + 1)/5 with x₀ = 0 to find x₃ to 4 d.p.
A bank balance follows Bₙ₊₁ = 1.04 Bₙ - 300 with B₀ = 6000. Find B₃.
Show that x³ - 5x + 1 = 0 has a root between 2 and 3.
independent: Core: a) Use x₍ₙ₊₁₎ = ∛(5xₙ - 1) with x₀ = 2 to find x₃ to 3 d.p. b) Show your starting equation was x³ = 5x - 1.
Extend: A tank holds 1000 litres. Each day 10% of the water is used and 80 litres are added. Write an iteration and find the amount after 3 days.
Stretch: Explain how to decide when to stop an iteration to give 2 d.p. accuracy.
exit: Use xₙ₊₁ = 2xₙ + 1 with x₀ = 1 to find x₃.
Explain why a sign change in f(x) shows a root.
Big question: How can repeating a simple calculation lead us to an exact-enough answer?
lessons.homework: Write your own iteration formula for 'a population grows by 5% then 20 are removed' and calculate three terms starting from 400.
lessons.send: SEND: use the Ans button and a table with columns n and xₙ. EAL: 'iteration', 'starting value'. Stretch: find which rearrangements of x³ - 5x + 1 = 0 converge. Higher-only: this whole lesson (R16).

lessons.unit: G9-G14: Geometry and measures: circles, solids and units
lessons.title: Parts of a circle and basic circle properties
lessons.bigQuestion: What can a single straight line tell us about a circle?
objectives: Name and use the parts of a circle
Use the radius-tangent and radius-chord properties
Use Pythagoras and isosceles triangles in circles
successCriteria: All: name chord, tangent, arc, sector and segment correctly
Most: find a chord length or distance using the perpendicular from the centre
Some: use the tangent-radius right angle to find lengths and angles
lessons.crossCurricular: Art and architecture: arches and domes
lessons.smsc: Order in creation: the circle in Islamic design.

keywords.def: a straight line joining two points on a circle
a straight line touching a circle at one point
the region between a chord and an arc

starter: Bismillah. Find the circumference of a circle of radius 5 cm in terms of π.
Use Pythagoras: legs 5 and 12, find the hypotenuse.
State the angle sum of a triangle.

teach.heading: Parts of a circle

head: Name
Meaning
rows: line joining two points on the circle
chord through the centre; the longest chord
between two radii and an arc
between a chord and an arc

teach.note: Show each on a diagram drawn live. Quick test: point at a region and ask for the name. Common mix-up: sector (pizza slice) and segment (cut off by a chord).
bullets: The perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord
A tangent is perpendicular to the radius
Triangles with two radii are isosceles

teach.heading: A chord and the centre

model.problem: A circle has centre O and radius 13 cm. The perpendicular from O to chord AB is 5 cm long. Find AB.
steps: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord

teach.note: Draw the right-angled triangle with hypotenuse the radius. Ask why we know it is right-angled. Reverse: given a chord of 16 cm in a circle of radius 10 cm, the distance is 6 cm.

teach.heading: A tangent

model.problem: PT is a tangent to a circle with centre O, touching at T. OT = 6 cm and OP = 10 cm. Find PT.
steps: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact
Triangle OTP has a right angle at T

teach.note: Reason to write: tangent perpendicular to radius. Ask what changes if the point P moves further away (PT grows).

teach.heading: Hinge: the chord

check.q: A chord of 16 cm is in a circle of radius 10 cm. The distance of the chord from the centre is:
check.why: Half the chord is 8 and the radius is 10, so the distance is √(100 - 64) = 6. 8 uses half chord only; 2 subtracts 10 - 8; 12 adds.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for the full reasoning: perpendicular bisects the chord.

teach.heading: Isosceles triangles

model.problem: O is the centre. A and B are on the circle and angle AOB = 70°. Find angle OAB.
steps: OA = OB (radii) so triangle OAB is isosceles

teach.note: Always mark equal radii on the diagram. This 'two radii' idea is used in all circle-theorem proofs. ANSWERS: practice: 6 cm; 5 cm; 40°; segment and sector. exit: 5 cm; the diameter. core: 9 cm; 15 cm; 60°. extend: r = √(49 + 16) = √65 ≈ 8.06 cm. stretch: PA = √(169 - 25) = 12 so area = 2 × ½ × 5 × 12 = 60 cm². homework: 8 cm.

practice: A circle has radius 10 cm. A chord is 16 cm long. Find its distance from the centre.
PT is a tangent. PT = 12 cm and OP = 13 cm. Find the radius.
O is the centre and angle AOB = 100°. Find angle OAB.
Name the region of a circle cut off by a chord, and the region between two radii.
independent: Core: a) A chord AB is 24 cm in a circle of radius 15 cm. Find the distance from the centre. b) A tangent from a point 17 cm from the centre of a circle with radius 8 cm: find the tangent length. c) OAB with OA = OB = AB = 6: find angle AOB.
Extend: A chord of length 14 cm is 4 cm from the centre. Find the radius to 3 s.f.
Stretch: Circle radius 5 cm. Tangents from P meet the circle at A and B and OP = 13. Find the area of quadrilateral OAPB.
exit: The radius is 13 cm and a chord is 24 cm: find its distance from the centre.
Which chord is the longest in a circle?
Big question: What can a single straight line tell us about a circle?
lessons.homework: A chord of length 30 cm lies in a circle of radius 17 cm. Find the distance from the centre. Then draw the diagram with all lengths marked.
lessons.send: SEND: use a pre-drawn diagram with the right angle marked, colour the radius and the half-chord. EAL: 'chord', 'tangent', 'segment', 'sector'. Stretch: derive the chord length formula in terms of radius and angle.

lessons.unit: G9-G14: Geometry and measures: circles, solids and units
lessons.title: Circle theorems 1: angles at the centre and circumference
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is the angle at the centre exactly double the angle at the edge?
objectives: State and use the angle at the centre theorem
Use the angle in a semicircle and angles in the same segment
Give correct reasons for each step
successCriteria: All: find angles using the theorems and give the reason
Most: combine theorems with isosceles triangles and algebra
Some: spot which theorem to use in a diagram
lessons.crossCurricular: Art: geometric design
lessons.smsc: Care with precision: justify every step with a stated reason.

keywords.def: an angle is subtended by an arc when its lines meet the ends of the arc
region between a chord and an arc
the boundary of the circle

starter: Find the angle sum of a quadrilateral.
In an isosceles triangle with apex angle 80°, find a base angle.
State what is special about the angle in a semicircle.

teach.heading: Theorems and the reason to write

head: Theorem
Reason to write
rows: Angle at the centre = 2 × angle at the circumference (same arc)
Angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference
Angle in a semicircle is a right angle
Angles in the same segment are equal

teach.note: Higher only. Describe diagrams aloud or draw them on a shared whiteboard: points A, B, C on the circle with centre O. Pupils must write the reason in full. The first theorem works only when both angles stand on the same arc AB.
bullets: Both angles on the same arc

teach.heading: Angle at the centre

model.problem: A, B and C lie on a circle with centre O. C is on the major arc AB. Angle AOB = 110°. Find angle ACB.
steps: Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference

teach.note: Check that C is on the major arc. Use the reverse: if ACB = 48° then AOB = 96°.

teach.heading: Angle in a semicircle

model.problem: AB is a diameter and C is on the circle. Angle CAB = 34°. Find angle ABC.

teach.note: Use the angle-sum of a triangle after the theorem. Ask which triangle is formed by a diameter and any point on the circle.

teach.heading: Hinge: angle at centre

check.q: Angle AOB at the centre is 140°. The angle ACB at the circumference (C on the major arc) is:
check.why: Half of 140° = 70°. 280° doubles instead; 35° halves again; 140° ignores the theorem.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask what is the angle at the centre if the angle at the circumference is 35° (70°).

teach.heading: Same segment

model.problem: C and D are on the same side of chord AB. Angle ACB = 48°. Find angle ADB and angle AOB, where O is the centre.
steps: Angles in the same segment are equal: ADB = 48°

teach.note: Both C and D 'look' at the same chord from the same side. Ask: what if D were on the other side? (180° - 48° = 132°, cyclic quadrilateral next lesson). ANSWERS: practice: 55°; 96°; 56°; 48°. exit: 42°; 90°. core: 6x + 10 = 2(2x + 15) so x = 10, AOB = 70° and ACB = 35°; 3x + 2x + 10 = 90 so x = 16. extend: AOB = 180 - 50 = 130° so ACB = 65°. stretch: reflex AOB = 260° so ACB = 130°, or 180° - 50° by opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral. homework: written reasons.

practice: A, B, C are on a circle with centre O. Angle AOB = 110° (C on the major arc). Find angle ACB.
Angle ACB = 48°. Find angle AOB.
AB is a diameter, angle CAB = 34°. Find angle ABC.
Angle ACB = 48° and D is on the same segment. Find angle ADB.
independent: Core: a) Angle AOB = 6x + 10 and angle ACB = 2x + 15. Find x and both angles. b) AB is a diameter. Angle CAB = 3x and angle ABC = 2x + 10. Find x.
Extend: O is the centre. Angle OAB = 25°. Find the angle ACB with C on the major arc.
Stretch: C is on the minor arc AB. Angle AOB (non-reflex) = 100°. Find angle ACB and explain.
exit: Angle AOB at the centre is 84°. Find the angle at the circumference.
AB is a diameter. State the size of angle ACB.
Big question: Why is the angle at the centre exactly double the angle at the edge?
lessons.homework: Write the reason you would give for each: 'angle at the centre = 2 × angle at the circumference', 'angle in a semicircle', 'angles in the same segment'. Create one example for each.
lessons.send: SEND: provide printed diagrams and a reason bank to choose from; colour the arcs. EAL: 'subtended', 'segment', 'circumference'. Stretch: combine two theorems in one problem. Higher-only: this whole lesson (G10).

lessons.unit: G9-G14: Geometry and measures: circles, solids and units
lessons.title: Circle theorems 2: cyclic quadrilaterals, tangents and the alternate segment
lessons.bigQuestion: How do tangents and chords combine to give angle facts?
objectives: Use the cyclic quadrilateral theorem
Use tangent facts: radius and equal tangents
Use the alternate segment theorem
successCriteria: All: find angles in a cyclic quadrilateral
Most: use tangent properties to find lengths and angles
Some: apply the alternate segment theorem with reasons
lessons.crossCurricular: Design: tessellations and arcs
lessons.smsc: Rigour: clearly stated reasons earn full marks in an exam.

keywords.def: a quadrilateral with all four vertices on a circle
the segment on the opposite side of the chord from the angle
touches the circle at one point

starter: Find the angle sum of a quadrilateral.
State what the angle between a tangent and a radius is.

teach.heading: Theorems and reasons

head: Theorem
Reason to write
rows: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°
Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral
Tangent is perpendicular to the radius
Tangents from an external point are equal
Tangents from a point are equal in length
Angle between tangent and chord = angle in the alternate segment
Perpendicular from centre bisects a chord
Perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord

teach.note: Higher only. Pupils build a revision card with a sketch of each. For the alternate segment theorem describe: a tangent TP at P and chord PQ; the angle TPQ equals the angle PRQ at any R on the opposite side of the chord.
bullets: Always state the theorem

teach.heading: Cyclic quadrilateral

model.problem: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. Angle ABC = 105° and angle DAB = 82°. Find angles ADC and BCD.

teach.note: Check that all four angles add to 360°: 82 + 105 + 98 + 75 = 360.

teach.heading: Alternate segment

model.problem: TP is a tangent to a circle at P. PQ is a chord and R is a point on the circle in the alternate segment. Angle TPQ = 62°. Find angle PRQ.
steps: The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment

teach.note: The 'alternate' segment is on the other side of the chord from the angle. Ask pupils to mark the tangent, chord, and the angle in the opposite segment in two colours.

teach.heading: Hinge: cyclic quadrilateral

check.q: In a cyclic quadrilateral, one angle is 96°. The angle opposite it is:
check.why: Opposite angles add to 180°, so 180° - 96° = 84°. 96° is a parallelogram property; 264° adds to 360°.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask what adjacent angles do (no rule).

teach.heading: Tangents from a point

model.problem: Tangents from T touch a circle at A and B. Angle ATB = 50°. Find angle TAB.
steps: Tangents from a point are equal: TA = TB

teach.note: Link with tangent-radius to build a kite OATB with two right angles at A and B: angle AOB = 130°. ANSWERS: practice: 75° and 98°; 62°; 65°; 38°. exit: 84°; 90°. core: 6x + 30 = 180 so x = 25 and A = 100°, C = 80°; 5y + 40 = 180 so y = 28 and B = 94°, D = 86°. extend: angle at circumference 70° so POQ = 140°; check: triangle OPQ has base angles 20° and 20° + 70° = 90° at P. stretch: angles at B = 75° and C = 40° by alternate segment; A = 65°. homework: by the angle at the centre argument.

practice: ABCD is cyclic: angle ABC = 105° and angle DAB = 82°. Find ADC and BCD.
TP is a tangent at P and PQ is a chord. Angle TPQ = 62°. Find the angle in the alternate segment.
Tangents TA and TB with angle ATB = 50°. Find angle TAB.
TA is a tangent, O is the centre, angle AOT = 52°. Find angle ATO.
independent: Core: a) ABCD cyclic: angle A = 4x, angle C = 2x + 30. Find x and the angles. b) Opposite angles B = 3y + 10, D = 2y + 30: find y.
Extend: TP is a tangent, PQ a chord, angle QPT = 70°. Find the angle POQ at the centre O.
Stretch: Triangle ABC is inscribed in a circle. The tangent at A makes angles of 40° with AB and 75° with AC on opposite sides. Find the three angles of the triangle.
exit: In a cyclic quadrilateral two opposite angles are 96° and y. Find y.
State the angle between a tangent and the radius at the point of contact.
Big question: How do tangents and chords combine to give angle facts?
lessons.homework: Explain, using two theorems, why the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°.
lessons.send: SEND: provide the five theorem cards with diagrams and let pupils match; colour-code the tangent. EAL: 'alternate', 'opposite', 'tangent'. Stretch: multi-step problems chaining three theorems. Higher-only: this whole lesson (G10).

lessons.unit: G9-G14: Geometry and measures: circles, solids and units
lessons.title: Proving the circle theorems
lessons.bigQuestion: Why are the circle theorems true for every circle?
objectives: Prove the angle at the centre theorem
Deduce the semicircle and cyclic quadrilateral theorems
Prove the alternate segment theorem
successCriteria: All: follow and reproduce a proof with reasons
Most: use a proved theorem to prove another
Some: write a proof in a clear sequence
lessons.crossCurricular: Logic: deduction and proof
lessons.smsc: Honesty in argument: every step must be justified.

keywords.def: show with logical steps that a statement is always true
reach a conclusion from known facts
an angle greater than 180°

starter: State the exterior angle theorem for a triangle.
In triangle OAC with OA = OC, angle OAC = x. Find angle OCA.
State the angle sum of a triangle.

teach.heading: Proof: angle at the centre

model.problem: Prove that the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference. Take A, B, C on a circle with centre O, with O inside the angle ACB.
steps: Join CO and extend to D. OA = OC (radii) so angle OAC = angle OCA = x
Angle AOD is an exterior angle of triangle OAC so AOD = 2x
Similarly OB = OC gives angle OBC = angle OCB = y and BOD = 2y

teach.note: Higher only. Draw clearly; label the isosceles triangles. The exterior angle theorem does the work. Say that this proof covers the main case; other positions of O can be handled in the same way.

teach.heading: Proof: angle in a semicircle

model.problem: Use the angle at the centre theorem to prove that the angle in a semicircle is a right angle.
steps: If AB is a diameter, the angle at the centre AOB is 180° (a straight line)
The angle at the circumference ACB is half of 180°

teach.note: A one-line deduction. Ask pupils to write each step with its reason. Show it is a special case of the first proof.

teach.heading: Proof: cyclic quadrilateral

model.problem: Prove that opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD add to 180°.
steps: Let angle ABC = x with B on the minor arc AC. The reflex angle AOC = 2x

teach.note: Uses the theorem twice: once for the angle at B and once for D on the other arc. Compare with the numerical examples in the previous lesson.

teach.heading: Hinge: reason bank

check.q: Which statement justifies 'angle OAC = angle OCA' in the proof?
options: Angles in a triangle sum to 180°
OA = OC as radii, so base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal
The tangent is perpendicular to the radius
check.why: OA and OC are radii, so triangle OAC is isosceles. The other options are true facts but they do not justify this step.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Stress that a reason must connect to the specific step.

teach.heading: Proof: alternate segment

model.problem: TP is a tangent at P and PQ is a chord. R is on the circle in the alternate segment. Prove angle TPQ = angle PRQ.
steps: Draw the diameter PS. Angle SPT = 90° (tangent perpendicular to radius), so angle SPQ = 90° - angle TPQ
Angle PQS = 90° (angle in a semicircle) so angle PSQ = 180° - 90° - (90° - TPQ) = TPQ
Angle PSQ = angle PRQ (angles in the same segment)

teach.note: The longest proof: ask pupils to draw it in stages. It builds on three earlier facts. Treat it as a stretch for most. ANSWERS: practice: angle AOB = 180° so ACB = 90°; proof as modelled; proof as modelled; ADC = 80°. exit: the angle at the centre theorem; join C to O and extend, using radii equal. core: (a) OA = OB (radii), OT common, right angles at A and B so RHS gives TA = TB; (b) OA = OB so triangle OAB isosceles and the perpendicular from O bisects AB by symmetry (or by RHS congruence). extend: base angles = 90° - x. stretch: angle at S equals angle PRQ if R is on the same segment as S; otherwise use the cyclic quadrilateral. homework: any correct proof.

practice: Write out the proof of the angle in a semicircle theorem using the first theorem.
Prove that the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference. Label the diagram.
ABCD is cyclic. Use the first theorem to prove opposite angles add to 180°.
Use the proof of the cyclic quadrilateral to find angle ADC if angle ABC = 100°.
independent: Core: a) Prove two tangents from a point T are equal in length (use right-angled triangles OAT and OBT). b) Prove the perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord.
Extend: In a circle with centre O, A and B are on the circle. Prove that the triangle OAB is isosceles and find the base angle if angle AOB = 2x.
Stretch: Complete the alternate segment proof when R is on the other segment.
exit: State which theorem proves that angle ACB = 90° for a diameter AB.
What is the first step in the proof of the angle at the centre theorem?
Big question: Why are the circle theorems true for every circle?
lessons.homework: Write the proof of the cyclic quadrilateral theorem in your own words, with reasons for every step.
lessons.send: SEND: provide proof scaffolds with statements and gaps for the reasons. EAL: sentence frames 'so', 'because', 'therefore'. Stretch: consider other positions of O. Higher-only: this whole lesson (G10, prove).

lessons.unit: G9-G14: Geometry and measures: circles, solids and units
lessons.title: Coordinate geometry: lengths, midpoints and gradients
lessons.bigQuestion: How can coordinates prove facts about shapes?
objectives: Find the distance between two points and the midpoint
Use gradients to show lines are parallel or perpendicular
Find equations of lines and solve geometric problems
successCriteria: All: find the distance, midpoint and gradient between two points
Most: find the equation of a parallel or perpendicular line
Some: prove a property of a shape using coordinates
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: graphics and coordinates
lessons.smsc: Rigour: deduce a conclusion from numbers, not from a picture.

keywords.def: the point halfway between two points
change in y ÷ change in x
at right angles

starter: Find the length of the hypotenuse with legs 6 and 8.

teach.heading: Four tools
bullets: Distance = √((x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)²)
Midpoint = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2)
Parallel lines: equal gradients
Perpendicular lines: gradients multiply to -1
teach.note: The distance formula is Pythagoras on a right-angled triangle drawn on the grid. Remind pupils that perpendicular gradient is the negative reciprocal: 2/3 becomes -3/2.

teach.heading: A line segment

model.problem: A(1, 2) and B(7, 10). Find the length of AB, its midpoint, and the equation of its perpendicular bisector.

teach.note: Check: at x = 4, y = -3 + 9 = 6 ✓. The perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint at right angles. Link to constructions and loci.

teach.heading: Hinge: perpendicular gradient

check.q: A line has gradient 2/3. The gradient of a perpendicular line is:
check.why: Negative reciprocal: -3/2. -2/3 changes only the sign; 3/2 changes only the fraction.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Check: 2/3 × (-3/2) = -1.

teach.heading: Prove a right angle

model.problem: P(1, 1), Q(4, 2), R(2, 8). Show triangle PQR has a right angle at Q and find its area.

teach.note: Show both gradients and the product. The area formula uses the two perpendicular sides. Alternative: use distances with Pythagoras.

teach.heading: A parallelogram

model.problem: A(0, 0), B(4, 1), C(6, 5), D(2, 4). Show that ABCD is a parallelogram.
steps: Opposite sides equal and parallel so ABCD is a parallelogram

teach.note: A second method: midpoints of AC and BD are both (3, 2.5). Ask if it is a rhombus (AB = √17, BC = √20: no). ANSWERS: practice: AB = 10, midpoint (5, 7), gradient 4/3; y = 3x - 1 and y = -x/3 + 7/3; AB = DC = (4, 1) and AD = BC = (2, 4); gradients 1/3 and -3. exit: 13; -4/3. core: (2, 3); 10; y = 2x - 2. extend: y = -3/4 x + 9. stretch: S = P + R - Q = (4, 5). homework: AB = (4, 2), DC = (4, 2) and AD = (-1, 4), BC = (-1, 4): parallelogram; AB = √20 and BC = √17: not a rhombus.

practice: A(2, 3) and B(8, 11): find the length of AB, its midpoint and its gradient.
Find the equation of the line through (1, 2) with gradient 3, and the perpendicular line through the same point.
Show that A(0, 0), B(4, 1), C(6, 5), D(2, 4) is a parallelogram.
Show that P(1, 1), Q(4, 2), R(2, 8) has a right angle at Q.
independent: Core: a) Midpoint of (-2, 5) and (6, 1). b) Distance from (-3, 4) to (5, -2). c) Equation of the line parallel to y = 2x - 3 through (3, 4).
Extend: Find the perpendicular bisector of A(1, 2) and B(7, 10).
Stretch: P(1, 1), Q(5, 2) and R(8, 6) are three vertices of a parallelogram PQRS. Find S.
exit: Find the distance from (0, 0) to (5, 12).
A line has gradient 3/4. State the gradient of a line perpendicular to it.
Big question: How can coordinates prove facts about shapes?
lessons.homework: Show that A(1, 1), B(5, 3), C(4, 7) and D(0, 5) form a parallelogram, and decide whether it is a rhombus.
lessons.send: SEND: use a coordinate grid with the triangle drawn; set out the formula with a coloured template. EAL: 'midpoint', 'perpendicular', 'parallelogram'. Stretch: find the circumcentre of a triangle. Higher-only: perpendicular gradients and perpendicular bisectors. Foundation: distance, midpoint, parallel lines.

lessons.unit: G9-G14: Geometry and measures: circles, solids and units
lessons.title: 3D solids, plans and elevations
lessons.bigQuestion: How can three flat drawings describe a solid?
objectives: Name solids and count faces, edges and vertices
Draw the plan and elevations of a solid
Use Euler's formula
successCriteria: All: count faces, edges and vertices
Most: draw plan, front and side elevations
Some: reconstruct a solid from its views
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and technology: technical drawing
lessons.smsc: Care in construction: the same plans and elevations let others build exactly what was designed.

keywords.def: the view from above
a view from the front or the side
a corner where edges meet

starter: Name the solid with a square base and four triangular faces.
How many faces does a cube have?
Find the volume of a cuboid 4 cm × 3 cm × 2 cm.

teach.heading: Faces, edges and vertices
teach.note: Euler's formula V - E + F = 2 works for polyhedra: cube 8 - 12 + 6 = 2; pentagonal prism 10 - 15 + 7 = 2. Cylinder: 2 flat faces and one curved. Ask pupils to predict the edges of a hexagonal prism (18).
bullets: Euler: V - E + F = 2 for polyhedra

teach.heading: A stack of cubes

model.problem: Five cubes: three in a row left to right on a table, and two more stacked on top of the left cube. Describe the plan, front elevation and side elevation (right).
steps: Plan (from above): a row of 3 squares
Front elevation: left column 3 squares high, then two columns each 1 square high
Side elevation from the right: one column 1 square wide and 3 high (the tall stack hides nothing)
model.answer: Plan: 1 × 3 row. Front: heights 3, 1, 1. Side: 1 wide, 3 high

teach.note: Draw them on squared paper or in a shared whiteboard. Ask: if the extra cubes were in front, would the plan change? (no). Elevations use the silhouette of the solid.

teach.heading: A prism

model.problem: A triangular prism lies on a rectangular face 4 cm by 10 cm. The cross-section is a right-angled triangle with a horizontal leg of 4 cm and a vertical leg of 3 cm. The length is 10 cm. Describe the three views.
steps: Plan: a rectangle 4 cm by 10 cm
Front elevation (looking at the triangular end): a right-angled triangle, base 4 cm and height 3 cm
Side elevation: a rectangle 10 cm by 3 cm
model.answer: Plan 4 × 10; front triangle 4 and 3; side rectangle 10 × 3

teach.note: Mention lines meeting at the corners and hidden edges as dotted lines. Cylinder standing up: plan circle, elevations rectangles; cone: plan circle with a centre dot, elevations triangles.

teach.heading: Hinge: counting edges

check.q: How many edges has a triangular prism?
check.why: 3 edges on each triangle and 3 joining them: 3 + 3 + 3 = 9. 6 counts only the triangles; 12 is a cube.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Check with Euler: 6 - 9 + 5 = 2.

teach.heading: Hidden parts

misconception.wrong: The side view of a stack must show all the cubes at their depths.
misconception.right: An elevation shows only the outline from one direction: the tallest stack in each line of sight.

teach.note: Check the stack of cubes again: the right view is a single column of height 3. ANSWERS: practice: hexagonal prism: F 8, E 18, V 12 so 12 - 18 + 8 = 2; E = V + F - 2 = 24; plan a rectangle 4 by 3, front elevation a rectangle 4 by 2; plan a circle of radius 3 cm with a centre dot, elevation isosceles triangles base 6 and height 5. exit: F 5, E 8, V 5; a circle. core: plan a row of 2 squares, front elevation columns of height 3 and 1, side elevation a 1 by 3 rectangle; a square-based pyramid. extend: plan a 6 cm square with diagonals; front elevation an isosceles triangle base 6 cm and height 4 cm. stretch: a 2 × 2 × 3 cuboid is one answer. homework: sketches checked against the object.

practice: Complete a table for a hexagonal prism: faces, edges, vertices, and check Euler's formula.
A polyhedron has 10 faces and 16 vertices. Find the number of edges.
Draw the plan and front elevation of a cuboid 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm standing on its 4 cm by 3 cm face.
Describe the plan and elevations of a cone of base radius 3 cm and height 5 cm standing on its base.
independent: Core: a) A solid of 4 cubes has two cubes side by side on the table and two more stacked on top of the left cube. Draw its plan, front elevation and side elevation. b) Describe the solid with plan a square with diagonals and elevations isosceles triangles.
Extend: A square-based pyramid has base 6 cm and vertical height 4 cm. Draw the plan and the front elevation, giving the dimensions.
Stretch: A solid has plan a 2 × 2 square and front and side elevations both a 3 × 2 rectangle. What could it be?
exit: How many faces, edges and vertices has a square-based pyramid?
State the plan view of a sphere.
Big question: How can three flat drawings describe a solid?
lessons.homework: Draw the plan, front and side elevations of an object at home that is made from cuboids, with measurements to the nearest centimetre.
lessons.send: SEND: use linking cubes and isometric paper; give the cube stack as a physical model. EAL: 'plan', 'elevation', 'vertex', 'edge'. Stretch: reconstruct a solid from three views with hidden lines.

lessons.unit: G9-G14: Geometry and measures: circles, solids and units
lessons.title: Units, estimation and dimensions of formulae
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we tell whether a formula gives a length, an area or a volume without using numbers?
objectives: Choose and convert standard units sensibly
Estimate quantities using known reference values
Use dimensions to check formulae for length, area and volume
successCriteria: All: use appropriate units for measures and money and time
Most: estimate a quantity using sensible rounded values
Some: decide whether an expression represents a length, an area or a volume
lessons.crossCurricular: Science and Design: dimensional analysis
lessons.smsc: Honest measurement: use the right unit, state it, and avoid false precision.

keywords.def: the number of lengths multiplied in a quantity: length 1, area 2, volume 3
an approximate value found using rounded numbers
all measurements in the same unit before calculating

teach.heading: Dimensions of expressions

head: Expression
Type of quantity
Dimension
rows: not valid: mixes area and length

teach.note: Higher only. Letters a, b, c and r are lengths; π and numbers have no dimension. Multiplying adds dimensions; adding or subtracting needs the same dimension. Ask: what is 4πr²? (area). 2πr + h? (length).
bullets: Add: same dimension only

teach.heading: Hinge: volume

check.q: a, b and r are lengths. Which expression could be a volume?
check.why: πa²b has three lengths multiplied (a, a, b). πab is an area; 2πa + b is a length; a² + b mixes area and length so is not valid.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for another volume expression, e.g. (4/3)πr³.

teach.heading: Estimation

model.problem: Estimate the mass of water in a swimming pool of length 25 m, width 10 m and average depth 2 m. (1 m³ of water has mass 1000 kg.)

teach.note: Reference values: height of a door about 2 m; adult mass about 70 kg; water 1 kg per litre. Say it is estimated, not exact.

teach.heading: Money and time

model.problem: Assume £1 = 65 EGP. A 780 EGP book is on sale. Find its price in pounds. A film begins at 19:45 and lasts 2 h 36 min: when does it end?

teach.note: Use the rate (per) idea, and add hours then minutes. This exchange rate is an assumption, not the current rate. Check: 12 × 65 = 780.

teach.heading: Mixed units

misconception.wrong: A room is 4.2 m long and 350 cm wide, so the area is 4.2 × 350 = 1470 m².
misconception.right: Use consistent units: 350 cm = 3.5 m, so area = 4.2 × 3.5 = 14.7 m² (or 420 × 350 = 147 000 cm²).

teach.note: Estimate first: about 4 m by 3.5 m is 14 m²; 1470 m² is wildly too large. ANSWERS: practice: ab area, a + b + c length, abc/a = bc area, a² + c invalid; 15p per 100 g; 1200 kg/m³ and 2500 cm²; sensible estimate such as 4 m × 5 m × 2.5 m = 50 m³. exit: area; 18 km/h. core: 2πr(r + h) is area (length²); πr²h is volume; 2πr is length and πr² is area so cannot be added. extend: 2 m × 1 m × 1 m = 2 000 000 cm³ so about 2 million cubes. stretch: πr²l/3 is a volume but r is a length so adding r is invalid. homework: 2.6 h × 85 = 221 km; speed: length per time; density: mass per volume; pressure: force per area.

practice: a, b, c are lengths. Say whether each is a length, an area, a volume or invalid: ab, a + b + c, abc/a, a² + c.
A rice bag of 2.4 kg costs £3.60. Find the price per 100 g.
Convert 1.2 g/cm³ into kg/m³ and 0.25 m² into cm².
Estimate the volume of air in your classroom or room at home (state your values).
independent: Core: a) A formula for the surface area of a closed cylinder is 2πr(r + h). State its dimension. b) V = πr²h: dimension. c) Show that 2πr + πr² cannot be a valid formula.
Extend: Estimate the number of 1 cm cubes needed to fill a 2 m by 1 m by 1 m skip.
Stretch: A formula claims the volume of a cone is πr²l/3 + r. Explain how dimensions show it is wrong.
exit: Is 4πr² a length, an area or a volume?
Convert 5 m/s into km/h.
Big question: How can we tell whether a formula gives a length, an area or a volume without using numbers?
lessons.homework: A journey takes 2 h 36 min at an average speed of 85 km/h. Find the distance. Then write the dimensions of speed, density and pressure in words ('length per time' etc.).
lessons.send: SEND: use a unit conversion chart and talk through estimation steps. EAL: 'dimension', 'length', 'area', 'volume'. Stretch: dimensions in physical formulae such as pressure = force ÷ area. Higher-only: dimensions of formulae.

lessons.unit: G20-G23: Geometry and measures: Pythagoras and trigonometry
lessons.title: Pythagoras' theorem
lessons.bigQuestion: How can the lengths of two sides tell us the third?
objectives: Use Pythagoras' theorem to find the hypotenuse or a shorter side
Use the converse to test for a right angle
Apply it to isosceles triangles, rectangles and coordinates
successCriteria: All: find the hypotenuse and a shorter side
Most: solve problems by drawing a right-angled triangle
Some: use the theorem for isosceles triangles and the converse
lessons.crossCurricular: Architecture and surveying: checking right angles
lessons.smsc: Mathematicians in Baghdad such as Thabit ibn Qurra (9th century) studied and generalised Pythagoras' theorem; we build on centuries of shared knowledge.

keywords.def: the longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle
three whole numbers that satisfy a² + b² = c²
using a² + b² = c² to prove a triangle has a right angle

teach.heading: The theorem
bullets: In a right-angled triangle a² + b² = c²
c is the hypotenuse: opposite the right angle
Add the squares to find the hypotenuse
Subtract to find a shorter side
teach.note: Draw squares on the three sides to show area meaning. Pupils always label the hypotenuse first. Triples worth recognising: 3, 4, 5; 5, 12, 13; 8, 15, 17; 7, 24, 25 and their multiples.

teach.heading: Finding a side

model.problem: A right-angled triangle has legs 8 cm and 15 cm. Find the hypotenuse. Another has hypotenuse 26 cm and one leg 10 cm. Find the other leg.

teach.note: Say 'add for the long side, subtract for a short side'. Check: the hypotenuse is always the longest side.

teach.heading: Hinge: which side?

check.q: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 13 cm and one leg 5 cm. The other leg is:
check.why: 13² - 5² = 169 - 25 = 144, so 12. √194 adds the squares (wrongly treating 13 as a leg); 8 subtracts the lengths; 18 adds them.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask how pupils know which method to use (hypotenuse is given).

teach.heading: An isosceles triangle

model.problem: An isosceles triangle has sides 10 cm, 10 cm and 12 cm. Find its height and area.
steps: Split into two right-angled triangles with base 6 cm and hypotenuse 10 cm

teach.note: The perpendicular from the apex bisects the base. This is the key trick for isosceles and equilateral triangles. Equilateral with side 8: height 4√3 and area 16√3.

teach.heading: The converse

model.problem: Is a triangle with sides 7 cm, 24 cm and 25 cm right-angled?
steps: They are equal so it is right-angled

teach.note: If the squares do not match it is not right-angled; the sign of the difference tells whether the angle is acute or obtuse. ANSWERS: practice: 17 cm; 24 cm; 48 cm²; 15 cm. exit: 13 cm; 16 cm. core: foot 2.71 m (√7.36); 36 + 64 = 100 not 121; distance 10. extend: half diagonals 5 and 12 so side 13 cm and perimeter 52 cm. stretch: height 4√3 ≈ 6.93 cm and area 16√3 ≈ 27.7 cm². homework: 100 m, saving 40 m.

practice: Legs 8 cm and 15 cm: find the hypotenuse.
Hypotenuse 26 cm, leg 10 cm: find the other leg.
An isosceles triangle has sides 10, 10 and 12 cm. Find the area.
A rectangle is 9 cm by 12 cm. Find the diagonal.
independent: Core: a) A 5 m ladder reaches 4.2 m up a wall. How far is the foot from the wall? b) Show that 6, 8 and 11 do not make a right-angled triangle. c) Find the distance between (1, 2) and (7, 10).
Extend: A rhombus has diagonals of 10 cm and 24 cm. Find its side length and perimeter.
Stretch: An equilateral triangle has side 8 cm. Find its height and area, leaving the answers in surd form.
exit: Legs 5 cm and 12 cm: find the hypotenuse.
Hypotenuse 20 cm, one leg 12 cm: find the other leg.
Big question: How can the lengths of two sides tell us the third?
lessons.homework: A field is a right-angled triangle with sides 60 m and 80 m. How much shorter is the diagonal path than walking along the two edges?
lessons.send: SEND: label the hypotenuse in colour and provide the formula frame; use calculators. EAL: 'hypotenuse', 'leg', 'square root'. Stretch: prove Pythagoras using a dissection.

lessons.unit: G20-G23: Geometry and measures: Pythagoras and trigonometry
lessons.title: Trigonometry in right-angled triangles
lessons.bigQuestion: How can an angle and one length give every other length?
objectives: Label the sides opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse
Use sine, cosine and tangent to find sides
Use inverse functions to find angles; use angles of elevation and depression
successCriteria: All: choose and use the correct ratio to find a side
Most: use an inverse ratio to find an angle
Some: solve problems with elevation and depression
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography and engineering: heights and slopes
lessons.smsc: Observation and calculation: measuring tall objects from the ground, as medieval astronomers did with astrolabes.

keywords.def: the side facing the angle
the side next to the angle that is not the hypotenuse
the angle above the horizontal

starter: Find the hypotenuse for legs 5 and 12.
Make sure your calculator is in degree mode: find sin 30°.

teach.heading: SOH CAH TOA
bullets: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse
cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse
tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent
Label the sides first, from the angle
teach.note: Label the sides on every question: hypotenuse opposite the right angle, opposite the angle, then adjacent. Choose the ratio that includes the known side and the unknown. Stress the calculator mode and the inverse functions sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹.

teach.heading: Finding a side

model.problem: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 12 cm and an angle of 35°. Find the side opposite the angle.
steps: Known: hypotenuse. Wanted: opposite. Use sin

teach.note: Multiply to move the unknown to the top. For an unknown on the bottom: 8 = ... divide: x = 8 ÷ tan 40° = 9.53 cm.

teach.heading: Finding an angle

model.problem: Opposite 5 cm and adjacent 9 cm. Find the angle θ.

teach.note: Check with a sketch: 5 is smaller than 9 so the angle is less than 45°. Another: adjacent 7, hypotenuse 10: cos θ = 0.7, θ = 45.6°.

teach.heading: Hinge: choosing the ratio

check.q: A right-angled triangle has opposite 5 and hypotenuse 13. To find the angle you use:
check.why: Opposite and hypotenuse give sin. tan⁻¹ would need opposite and adjacent; cos needs adjacent.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for the angle (22.6°) and the adjacent (12).

teach.heading: Angle of elevation

model.problem: From a point 40 m from the base of a tower on level ground, the angle of elevation of the top is 28°. Find the height of the tower.

teach.note: Draw the right-angled triangle with the horizontal. Add the observer's eye height if given. The angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the ground (alternate angles). ANSWERS: practice: 6.88 cm; 29.1°; 45.6°; 21.3 m. exit: 23.6°; 10 cm. core: 9.24; 9.53; 14.2. extend: tan⁻¹(1.2/10) = 6.8°. stretch: distance 60 ÷ tan 35° = 85.7 m; after moving 65.7 m the angle = tan⁻¹(60/65.7) ≈ 42.4°. homework: 4.5 × tan 40° ≈ 3.78 m.

practice: Hypotenuse 12 cm, angle 35°: find the side opposite.
Opposite 5 cm and adjacent 9 cm: find the angle.
Adjacent 7 cm and hypotenuse 10 cm: find the angle.
From a point 40 m from a tower the angle of elevation of the top is 28°. Find its height.
independent: Core: a) Find x = 15 cos 52°. b) Find x with tan 40° = 8/x. c) Find the hypotenuse with a side of 6 opposite 25°.
Extend: A ramp rises 1.2 m over a horizontal distance of 10 m. Find the angle of the ramp.
Stretch: From the top of a 60 m cliff the angle of depression of a boat is 35°. Find the distance of the boat from the base. The boat moves 20 m nearer; find the new angle of depression.
exit: sin θ = 0.4: find θ.
Hypotenuse 20 cm, angle 30°: find the opposite side.
Big question: How can an angle and one length give every other length?
lessons.homework: A lamp post casts a shadow of 4.5 m when the sun's elevation is 40°. Find its height. Draw the triangle.
lessons.send: SEND: use a triangle template with colours for opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse, and a flow chart for choosing a ratio. EAL: 'opposite', 'adjacent', 'elevation'. Stretch: bearings with trigonometry.

lessons.unit: G20-G23: Geometry and measures: Pythagoras and trigonometry
lessons.title: Exact trigonometric values
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do 30°, 45° and 60° have answers we can write exactly?
objectives: Know the exact values of sin, cos and tan for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°
Derive them from an equilateral triangle and a square
Use exact values in calculations without a calculator
successCriteria: All: recall the exact values
Most: use them to find exact lengths
Some: derive the values and use them in surd problems
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: angles in vectors and forces
lessons.smsc: Pattern and order: simple numbers behind special angles.

keywords.def: a value written using fractions and surds, not rounded
an irrational root such as √3
remove a surd from the denominator

teach.heading: Exact values
teach.note: Must be recalled without a calculator (non-calculator paper). Memory aid: sin 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° are √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2. Cos goes in reverse. tan = sin ÷ cos.
bullets: Cos is sin reversed
tan = sin ÷ cos

teach.heading: Deriving the values

model.problem: Use an equilateral triangle of side 2 split in half to find sin 30°, cos 30° and tan 60°.
steps: Half the triangle has hypotenuse 2, base 1, height √3 (Pythagoras: √(4 - 1))
Angle at the top is 30°, at the base 60°

teach.note: A unit square with diagonal √2 gives sin 45° = 1/√2 = √2/2 and tan 45° = 1. Pupils sketch both triangles.

teach.heading: Hinge: recall

check.q: The exact value of cos 60° is:
check.why: cos 60° = 1/2. √3/2 is sin 60° or cos 30°; √2/2 is cos 45°.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Use the equilateral-triangle sketch to check: adjacent 1, hypotenuse 2.

teach.heading: Using exact values

model.problem: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 10 cm and an angle of 60°. Find the opposite side exactly.

teach.note: Answer in surd form, which is what the question says by 'exact'. Check: 5√3 ≈ 8.66, which is a bit shorter than 10.

teach.heading: Exact area

model.problem: Find the exact area of an equilateral triangle of side 6 cm.

teach.note: Alternatively use Pythagoras: height = √(36 - 9) = √27 = 3√3. Compare with ½ab sin C = ½ × 6 × 6 × sin 60° = 9√3. ANSWERS: practice: 1/2, √2/2, √3; 3/4 + 1/4 = 1; 6 cm; 1/2. exit: √3/2 and √3/3; 4√2 cm. core: (√3/2) × √3 = 3/2; hyp 8 cm, opposite 4√3 cm. extend: 5√3 cm. stretch: (√2/2)(√2/2) = 2/4 = 1/2; hexagon = 6 × ½ × 4 × 4 × sin 60° = 24√3 cm². homework: the diagonal of a unit square is √2 so a 45° triangle has legs 1, 1 and hypotenuse √2 giving tan 45° = 1.

practice: Write the exact values of sin 30°, cos 45° and tan 60°.
Show that (sin 60°)² + (cos 60°)² = 1.
A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 12 cm and a 30° angle. Find the side opposite it, exactly.
Evaluate tan 45° × sin 30°.
independent: Core: a) cos 30° × tan 60°. b) A right-angled triangle has a 60° angle and adjacent side 4 cm. Find the hypotenuse and the opposite side exactly.
Extend: Find the exact height of an equilateral triangle of side 10 cm.
Stretch: Show that sin 45° × cos 45° = 1/2 and find the exact area of a regular hexagon of side 4 cm.
exit: Write the exact values of sin 60° and tan 30°.
A right-angled isosceles triangle has hypotenuse 8 cm. Find a leg exactly.
Big question: Why do 30°, 45° and 60° have answers we can write exactly?
lessons.homework: Explain, with a sketch, how to get tan 45° = 1 from a square.
lessons.send: SEND: provide the filled table and the two triangles as reference; ask for a pattern check. EAL: 'exact value', 'surd'. Stretch: derive exact values for 15° (not required). Higher: all values including tan 30° and tan 60°. Foundation requires fewer values (check against the specification).

lessons.unit: G20-G23: Geometry and measures: Pythagoras and trigonometry
lessons.title: Pythagoras and trigonometry in three dimensions
lessons.bigQuestion: How long is the longest rod that fits inside a box?
objectives: Use Pythagoras to find space diagonals
Find angles between a line and a plane
Solve problems in cuboids and pyramids
successCriteria: All: find a space diagonal using Pythagoras twice
Most: find the angle between a line and the base
Some: solve a pyramid problem in 3D
lessons.crossCurricular: Engineering: structures and storage
lessons.smsc: Efficiency and care in design: the right container for the right thing.

keywords.def: a diagonal joining opposite corners of a cuboid through the inside

keywords.term: angle between a line and a plane
keywords.def: the angle between the line and its projection on the plane
the top vertex of a pyramid

starter: A rectangle 8 cm by 6 cm: find its diagonal.
Opposite 5 and adjacent 10: find the angle.

teach.heading: Plan of attack
bullets: Draw the right-angled triangle you need, flat
Find one length at a time
Use Pythagoras for lengths and trigonometry for angles
The angle to a plane uses the triangle with the vertical height
teach.note: Higher only. Give pupils a cuboid net or a box to point at lines. Encourage: always draw the 2D triangle separately and label every side before choosing a method.

teach.heading: Space diagonal

model.problem: A cuboid is 8 cm by 6 cm by 5 cm. Find the space diagonal and the angle it makes with the base.
steps: Angle with the base: tan θ = 5 ÷ 10 so θ = 26.6°

teach.note: Pythagoras twice (or √(a² + b² + c²) in one go). The angle between the diagonal and the base is in the vertical triangle: base diagonal and height.

teach.heading: Hinge: space diagonal

check.q: A cuboid is 12 cm by 9 cm by 8 cm. The space diagonal is:
check.why: √(144 + 81 + 64) = √289 = 17. Adding the lengths gives 29; using only the base gives 15.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for the angle with the base (tan θ = 8/15, 28.1°).

teach.heading: A pyramid

model.problem: A square-based pyramid has base side 10 cm and vertical height 12 cm. Find the sloping edge and the angle the edge makes with the base.

teach.note: The foot of the height is the centre of the square base. Ask also for the angle between a sloping face and the base: tan = 12/5 gives 67.4°.

teach.heading: Wrong triangle

misconception.wrong: The angle between the edge and the base uses the sloping edge and the base side (10 cm).
misconception.right: The angle uses the edge and its projection on the base: from the centre of the base to the corner.

teach.note: Draw the vertical triangle: height, half-diagonal, edge. The base side is not involved. ANSWERS: practice: 11.2 cm and 26.6°; 13.9 cm and 59.5°; 67.4°; x = 12 (3² + 4² + 12² = 169). exit: 7 cm; draw the right-angled triangle from the line to its projection on the plane. core: (a) 17 cm; (b) √(4 + 2.25 + 1) = √7.25 = 2.69 m. extend: base diagonal 10 so half is 5; edge = √(144 + 25) = 13 cm. stretch: base diagonal 6√2, angle tan⁻¹(6/(6√2)) = tan⁻¹(1/√2) = 35.3°. homework: space diagonal √(4 + 2.25 + 1.44) = √7.69 = 2.77 m so 3 m does not fit.

practice: A cuboid is 8 cm by 6 cm by 5 cm. Find the space diagonal and its angle with the base.
A square-based pyramid has base 10 cm and height 12 cm. Find the sloping edge and its angle with the base.
For the same pyramid find the angle between a sloping face and the base.
A rod 13 cm long fits in a box 3 cm by 4 cm by x cm exactly along the space diagonal. Find x.
independent: Core: a) A cuboid 12 cm by 9 cm by 8 cm: find the space diagonal. b) A 2 m by 1.5 m by 1 m crate: find the longest rod it can hold.
Extend: A pyramid has a rectangular base 8 cm by 6 cm and vertical height 12 cm above the centre. Find the sloping edge.
Stretch: In a cube of side 6 cm, find the angle between the space diagonal and the base.
exit: A cuboid is 2 cm by 3 cm by 6 cm. Find its space diagonal.
State the first step to find the angle between a line and a plane.
Big question: How long is the longest rod that fits inside a box?
lessons.homework: A 3 m long pole is to be stored in a crate that is 2 m by 1.5 m by 1.2 m. Does it fit? Show your calculation.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a pre-drawn cuboid with the right-angled triangles marked in colour; physical boxes help. EAL: 'space diagonal', 'apex', 'plane'. Stretch: angle between two faces of a pyramid. Higher-only: this whole lesson (G20 in 3D).

lessons.unit: G20-G23: Geometry and measures: Pythagoras and trigonometry
lessons.title: The sine rule
lessons.bigQuestion: What can we do when a triangle has no right angle?
objectives: Use the sine rule to find a side
Use the sine rule to find an angle
Choose the correct rule for a triangle
successCriteria: All: find a missing side using the sine rule
Most: find a missing angle using the sine rule
Some: recognise when two triangles are possible (the ambiguous case)
lessons.crossCurricular: Surveying: measuring across a river or valley
lessons.smsc: Al-Biruni and other Muslim scholars used trigonometry to measure the Earth and find the direction of prayer; a skill that helps in worship and science.

keywords.def: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C
a is the side opposite angle A
when the given information fits two different triangles

starter: Rearrange x/sin 30° = 8/sin 45° to make x the subject.

teach.heading: The sine rule
bullets: a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B = c ÷ sin C
Each side is opposite its angle
Needs a matching side and angle pair
Use it for AAS, ASA or SSA
teach.note: Higher only. Label the triangle with capital letters for angles and the matching lowercase for opposite sides. For lengths use sides on top; for angles use the sines on top (flip the rule).

teach.heading: Finding a side

model.problem: In triangle ABC, A = 40°, B = 65° and a = 8 cm. Find b.

teach.note: Matching pair: a and A. Check that b is the larger side because B > A. Pupils sometimes pair a with B.

teach.heading: Finding an angle

model.problem: In triangle ABC, a = 11 cm, b = 9 cm and A = 48°. Find angle B.

teach.note: Because b < a, angle B must be smaller than A so B is acute. Mention the ambiguous case: if the given angle is opposite the shorter side two triangles may exist. Higher stretch.

teach.heading: Hinge: which rule?

check.q: A triangle has two angles and one side given. Which rule is used to find another side?
check.why: With two angles and any side we can find the third angle and use the sine rule. Pythagoras needs a right angle; the cosine rule needs two sides and the included angle, or three sides.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Add a second question: two sides and the included angle (cosine rule next).

teach.heading: Choosing a rule

head: Given
Find
Use
rows: Right angle, angle and a side
Two sides and an angle opposite one
Two sides and the included angle

teach.note: This table is the pupils' revision aid. Ask them to add an example for each row. The cosine rule is next lesson. ANSWERS: practice: 11.3 cm; 32.0°; AC ≈ 198 m (C = 70°, AC = 250 sin 48° ÷ sin 70°); b = 12.0 cm and c = 10.6 cm (C = 57°). exit: 8.49 cm (6√2); a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B = c ÷ sin C. core: sin B = 9 sin 40° ÷ 7 = 0.826 so B = 55.7° or 124.3°, so two triangles; third angle 105°, side = 6 × sin 45° ÷ sin 30° = 6√2 ≈ 8.49. extend: angle P = 180° - 48° - 66° = 66°, so QR = 12 cm and PR = 12 sin 48° ÷ sin 66° = 9.76 cm. stretch: proof using the diameter through a vertex. homework: pupil-set.
bullets: Match the rule to the information

practice: In triangle ABC, A = 40°, B = 65° and a = 8 cm. Find b.
a = 9.1 cm, b = 7.5 cm and A = 40°. Find angle B.
From two points A and B 250 m apart on one bank of a river, angle at A to a tree C on the other bank is 62° and at B is 48°. Find AC.
A = 52°, B = 71°, a = 10 cm. Find b and c.
independent: Core: a) a = 7, b = 9, A = 40°: find B. How many triangles are possible? b) Triangle with angles 30° and 45° and side 6 opposite 30°: find the other side exactly.
Extend: Triangle PQR: PQ = 12 cm, angle Q = 48°, angle R = 66°. Find PR and QR.
Stretch: Prove that the sine rule gives a = 2R sin A when the triangle is in a circle of radius R (extension: use a diameter).
exit: In triangle ABC, A = 30°, B = 45°, a = 6: find b.
State the sine rule.
Big question: What can we do when a triangle has no right angle?
lessons.homework: Write your own triangle problem where the sine rule is the correct method, and solve it.
lessons.send: SEND: use a fixed layout with the triangle labelled and a formula template; supply the rule table. EAL: 'opposite', 'matching pair'. Stretch: the ambiguous case with a diagram. Higher-only: this whole lesson (G22).

lessons.unit: G20-G23: Geometry and measures: Pythagoras and trigonometry
lessons.title: The cosine rule
lessons.bigQuestion: What can we do when we know two sides and the angle between them?
objectives: Use the cosine rule to find a side
Use the cosine rule to find an angle from three sides
Choose between the sine and cosine rules
successCriteria: All: find a missing side using the cosine rule
Most: find a missing angle using the rearranged cosine rule
Some: solve a real problem, such as two ships leaving a port
lessons.crossCurricular: Navigation: distances between two travellers
lessons.smsc: Safe travel: working out how far apart groups are.

keywords.def: a² = b² + c² - 2bc cos A
the angle between two given sides
an angle larger than 90°

teach.heading: The cosine rule
bullets: a² = b² + c² - 2bc cos A
Angle A is between sides b and c
To find an angle: cos A = (b² + c² - a²) ÷ 2bc
A negative cosine means an obtuse angle
teach.note: Higher only. Emphasise structure: Pythagoras plus a correction term. The side being found is opposite the angle in the formula. Calculator: use brackets and do cos before multiplying.

teach.heading: Finding a side

model.problem: In triangle ABC, b = 8 cm, c = 11 cm and A = 62°. Find a.

teach.note: Do not subtract before multiplying (the common slip of (64 + 121 - 176) × cos 62°). Check: a is slightly shorter than c, plausible for an angle of 62°.

teach.heading: Finding an angle

model.problem: In triangle ABC, a = 12 cm, b = 7 cm and c = 9 cm. Find angle A, the largest angle.

teach.note: A negative value is fine: the angle is obtuse. The largest angle is opposite the longest side, so check this.

teach.heading: Hinge: which rule?

check.q: A triangle has sides 7, 9 and 12 and no angles. To find an angle:
check.why: Three sides and no angle: cosine rule. Sine rule needs a matching side and angle pair.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Revisit the rule table from last lesson.

teach.heading: Two ships

model.problem: Ship A sails 12 km on a bearing of 040° and ship B sails 15 km on a bearing of 100° from the same port. How far apart are they?

teach.note: Draw the diagram with north lines and mark the 60° included angle. This is the typical exam bearing problem. ANSWERS: practice: 7 cm; 87.3°; 44.4°; 13.7 km. exit: 4.58 cm (√21); when the information is two sides and the included angle, or three sides. core: a² = 81 + 144 - 216 cos 100° = 262.5 so a = 16.2; cos x = (64 + 81 - 100) ÷ 144 = 0.3125 so 71.8°. extend: the largest angle is opposite 200 m: cos = (120² + 150² - 200²) ÷ (2 × 120 × 150) = -0.0861 so 94.9°. stretch: 48.2°, 58.4° and 73.4°. homework: angle between paths 90° so Pythagoras: 5 km.

practice: b = 5, c = 8, A = 60°: find a.
Triangle with sides 6, 7, 9: find the largest angle.
Sides 5, 6, 7: find the smallest angle.
Ships A and B: 12 km on 040° and 15 km on 100° from port. How far apart are they?
independent: Core: a) b = 9, c = 12 and A = 100°: find a. b) Sides 8, 9 and 10: find angle opposite 10.
Extend: A triangular field has sides 120 m, 150 m and 200 m. Find the largest angle.
Stretch: A triangle has sides 7 cm, 8 cm and 9 cm. Find all three angles and check they add to 180°.
exit: Sides 4 cm and 5 cm and the angle between them 60°: find the third side.
State when to use the cosine rule rather than the sine rule.
Big question: What can we do when we know two sides and the angle between them?
lessons.homework: Two walkers leave a car park on bearings 070° and 160°, walking 3 km and 4 km. How far apart are they?
lessons.send: SEND: give a worked layout in four lines with blanks; use a calculator carefully with brackets. EAL: 'included angle', 'obtuse'. Stretch: derive the cosine rule from Pythagoras with an altitude. Higher-only: this whole lesson (G22).

lessons.unit: G20-G23: Geometry and measures: Pythagoras and trigonometry
lessons.title: Area of a triangle ½ab sin C and mixed problems
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we find the area of a triangle without its height?
objectives: Use area = ½ab sin C
Find an angle from an area
Combine the sine rule, cosine rule and area formula in multi-step problems
successCriteria: All: find the area of a triangle from two sides and the included angle
Most: find an angle or side from a given area
Some: solve mixed triangle problems and segment areas
lessons.crossCurricular: Land surveying: area of fields
lessons.smsc: Fair measurement of land: accuracy matters for fair dealing.

keywords.def: Area = ½ab sin C
region between a chord and an arc
the angle between sides a and b

starter: State when to use the sine rule.

teach.heading: The formula
bullets: Area = ½ ab sin C
a and b are two sides; C is the angle between them
