Works for any triangle (needs no height)
Parallelogram area = ab sin C
teach.note: Higher only. Derive it from ½ × base × height where height = a sin C. Remind pupils that the angle must be between the two sides used. If it is not, find it first.

teach.heading: Finding an area

model.problem: Triangle ABC has sides 8 cm and 11 cm and included angle 62°. Find its area.

teach.note: Give to 3 s.f. Check with the alternative: base 11, height 8 sin 62° = 7.06, area = ½ × 11 × 7.06 = 38.8.

teach.heading: Finding an angle from the area

model.problem: A triangle has sides 10 cm and 8 cm and area 30 cm². Find the angle between them.

teach.note: The second solution is 180° - 48.6°; both give the same area. Say which is intended by the diagram or the word 'acute'.

teach.heading: Hinge: included angle

check.q: In triangle ABC, which angle should be used in ½ab sin C for sides AB and AC?
check.why: The angle must be between the two sides used. AB and AC meet at A.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask which sides go with angle B (AB and BC).

teach.heading: A mixed problem

model.problem: A triangle has sides 6 cm, 7 cm and 9 cm. Find the largest angle and the area.

teach.note: The cosine rule gives the included angle first. Compare with Heron's formula (not required): s = 11, area = √(11 × 5 × 4 × 2) = √440 = 21.0. ANSWERS: practice: 34.7 cm²; 36.9°; 16π - 32 ≈ 18.3 cm²; angle opposite 9: cos C = (25 + 49 - 81) ÷ 70 = -0.1 so 95.7° and area = ½ × 5 × 7 × sin 95.7° = 17.4 cm². exit: 30 cm²; because it is the angle enclosed by the two sides, otherwise the formula gives the wrong area. core: 6 × ½ × 6 × 6 × sin 60° = 54√3 ≈ 93.5 cm²; 8 × 5 × sin 70° = 37.6 cm². extend: sin A = 50 ÷ 63 = 0.794 so A = 52.5°. stretch: 6π - 9√3 ≈ 3.26 cm². homework: ½ × 80 × 120 × sin 55° = 3932 m² which is about 0.39 ha.

practice: Sides 9 cm and 12 cm with included angle 40°: find the area.
A triangle has sides 8 cm and 10 cm and area 24 cm². Find the acute angle between them.
A sector of radius 8 cm has angle 90°. Find the area of the segment.
A triangle has sides 5 cm, 7 cm and 9 cm. Find its largest angle and area.
independent: Core: a) Area of a regular hexagon of side 6 cm. b) A parallelogram has sides 8 cm and 5 cm and an angle of 70°: find its area.
Extend: A triangle ABC has AB = 7 cm, AC = 9 cm and area 25 cm². Find the acute angle at A.
Stretch: A sector has radius 6 cm and angle 60°: find the exact area of the segment.
exit: Triangle with sides 10 cm and 12 cm and included angle 30°: area.
Why must the angle in ½ab sin C be between the two sides?
Big question: How can we find the area of a triangle without its height?
lessons.homework: A triangular plot has sides 80 m and 120 m and an included angle of 55°. Find its area in square metres and in hectares (1 hectare = 10 000 m²).
lessons.send: SEND: provide a template with the triangle labelled and a calculator layout. EAL: 'included angle'. Stretch: show that the area of a regular n-sided polygon is ½ n r² sin(360°/n). Higher-only: this whole lesson (G23).

lessons.unit: G24-G25: Geometry and measures: vectors
lessons.title: Column vectors and translations
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a pair of numbers describe a movement?
objectives: Describe translations using column vectors
Find the vector between two points
Find the magnitude of a vector
successCriteria: All: write a translation as a column vector
Most: find the vector AB from coordinates
Some: calculate the magnitude of a vector
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: displacement
lessons.smsc: Journey and direction: a vector has both size and direction.

keywords.def: a quantity with magnitude and direction
numbers written in a column: top is x, bottom is y
the length of a vector

teach.heading: Column vectors
bullets: (3, -2) means 3 right and 2 down
A translation moves every point by the same vector
The vector AB goes from A to B
BA = -AB (opposite direction)
teach.note: Write column vectors vertically on the board. In text we write (3, -2) with the top number first. Ask pupils to show the vector on a grid and explain 'top number is horizontal'.

teach.heading: The vector between two points

model.problem: A is (2, 3) and B is (7, 1). Find the vector AB, the vector BA and the length of AB.

teach.note: End minus start. Pythagoras gives the magnitude. Ask for a vector parallel to AB and twice as long: (10, -4).

teach.heading: Translating a shape

model.problem: Translate the triangle (1, 1), (4, 1), (2, 3) by the vector (-3, 4).

teach.note: The image is congruent, with sides parallel to the originals. Describe a translation fully by its vector: no centre or angle is needed.

teach.heading: Hinge: the vector

check.q: The vector from (1, 6) to (4, 2) is:
check.why: End minus start: (4 - 1, 2 - 6) = (3, -4). (-3, 4) is the vector BA; (3, 4) forgets the sign.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for the length (5).

teach.heading: Scalar or vector?

right.title: Vector
points: Written as a column or bold letter

teach.note: Ask pupils for an example: 'run at 5 m/s' (speed, scalar) and '5 m/s north' (velocity, vector). Link to the physics course. ANSWERS: practice: (5, -2), (-5, 2), √29 ≈ 5.39; (-2, 5), (1, 5), (-1, 7); (6, -4); (-4, 4). exit: (5, -3); (-2, 3). core: A = (5, 7); (4, -2) and (0, 0) → (4, -2); 13; 50 km. homework: (4, -5) and √41 ≈ 6.40.

practice: A is (2, 3) and B is (7, 1). Find AB, BA and the length of AB.
Translate triangle (1, 1), (4, 1), (2, 3) by (-3, 4).
Find the vector from P(-2, 5) to Q(4, 1).
Describe the translation that maps the point (3, 5) to (-1, 9).
independent: Core: a) The translation (3, -2) maps A to (8, 5). Find A. b) A translation maps (2, 3) to (6, 1): describe it and apply it to (0, 0).
Extend: Find the magnitude of (-5, 12).
Stretch: A ship sails (30, 40) km east and north from port. How far is it from port?
exit: Find the vector from (0, 4) to (5, 1).
Translate (2, -3) by the vector (-4, 6).
Big question: How can a pair of numbers describe a movement?
lessons.homework: An object is moved by the vector (6, -8) and then by (-2, 3). What single vector does the same job? Find its size.
lessons.send: SEND: draw each vector on a grid with arrows; use coloured pens for x and y. EAL: 'vector', 'column', 'magnitude'. Stretch: vectors in three dimensions.

lessons.unit: G24-G25: Geometry and measures: vectors
lessons.title: Adding, subtracting and scaling vectors
lessons.bigQuestion: What happens when one movement follows another?
objectives: Add and subtract vectors using diagrams and columns
Multiply a vector by a scalar
Recognise parallel vectors
successCriteria: All: add and subtract two column vectors
Most: multiply by a scalar and find parallel vectors
Some: use the triangle law and resultants
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: resultant forces
lessons.smsc: Teamwork: combining efforts gives a resultant.

keywords.def: an ordinary number used to multiply a vector
the single vector equal to the combined effect
vectors that are scalar multiples of each other

teach.heading: Operations on vectors
bullets: Add or subtract component by component
Scalar multiple: multiply both components
a and ka are parallel
Triangle law: AB + BC = AC
teach.note: Draw the triangle law: moving from A to B then from B to C is the same as going straight from A to C. Subtraction a - b means a + (-b): reverse b.

teach.heading: Arithmetic

model.problem: Let a = (2, 3) and b = (-1, 4). Find 2a + 3b, a - b and |a - b|.

teach.note: Scale each vector first and then add. The magnitude uses the components of the result, not the sum of magnitudes.

teach.heading: Hinge: arithmetic

check.why: 3(2, -1) = (6, -3). Subtract (1, 4): (5, -7). (7, -7) adds; (5, 1) subtracts only the sign wrongly.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for the magnitude of the answer.

teach.heading: Parallel vectors

model.problem: Find k so that (k, 6) is parallel to (2, 3), and show that (6, -9) is parallel to (2, -3).

teach.note: Parallel means one is a scalar multiple of the other. Same direction if the scalar is positive; opposite if negative.

teach.heading: Resultant

model.problem: A boat travels (4, 3) then (-1, 5) then (2, -2). Find the resultant and the distance from the start.

teach.note: The resultant is the single vector for the whole journey. Draw the path as nose-to-tail arrows. ANSWERS: practice: (1, 18) and (3, -1); (5, -7); k = 4; (5, 6) and √61 ≈ 7.81. exit: (-2, 5); (4, -10). core: 2p - 3q = (6 + 12, -4 - 3) = (18, -7); p + q = (-1, -1) so magnitude √2; (-6, 9) = -1.5 × (4, -6) so parallel. extend: OB = OA + OC = (5, 3) and CB = OA = (4, 0). stretch: m + 3n = 7 and 2m - n = 4; from the second n = 2m - 4, so 7m - 12 = 7 and m = 19/7, n = 10/7. homework: such as (2, 1) + (3, -4) and (7, -3) + (-2, 0).

practice: Find k so that (k, 6) is parallel to (2, 3).
A boat travels (4, 3), (-1, 5), (2, -2): find the resultant and the distance from the start.
independent: Core: a) p = (3, -2), q = (-4, 1): find 2p - 3q and |p + q|. b) Are (4, -6) and (-6, 9) parallel?
Extend: OABC has OA = (4, 0) and OC = (1, 3). Find OB and CB where OABC is a parallelogram.
Stretch: Find the values of m and n if m(1, 2) + n(3, -1) = (7, 4).
exit: Find a vector parallel to (2, -5) with magnitude double.
Big question: What happens when one movement follows another?
lessons.homework: Write down two different pairs of vectors whose sum is (5, -3). Draw one pair as a triangle.
lessons.send: SEND: use squared paper and draw each vector as an arrow before calculating. EAL: 'scalar', 'resultant', 'parallel'. Stretch: simultaneous equations from a vector equation.

lessons.unit: G24-G25: Geometry and measures: vectors
lessons.title: Vectors in geometry and proof
lessons.bigQuestion: Can vectors prove things about shapes without a diagram?
objectives: Express vectors in a diagram in terms of a and b
Find the position of a point dividing a line in a ratio
Use vectors to show lines are parallel or points are collinear
successCriteria: All: write vectors for the sides and diagonals of a figure
Most: find a midpoint or a division point
Some: prove a geometric result such as the midpoint theorem
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics and computing: vectors in graphics
lessons.smsc: Logical proof: deduction that does not rely on a drawing.

keywords.def: lying on the same straight line
the vector from the origin O to a point
a point splitting a line in a given ratio

starter: Write AB in terms of OA and OB.

teach.heading: Building vector routes
bullets: Go from one point to another by any path along known vectors
AB = OB - OA = b - a
Reverse a vector: BA = -AB
Midpoint M of AB: OM = ½(a + b)
teach.note: Higher only. Draw OAB with OA = a and OB = b. The key technique: express every unknown vector as a route along known vectors. A scalar multiple relationship proves parallel lines; a common point plus a multiple proves collinear points.

teach.heading: Midpoint and ratio

model.problem: OA = a and OB = b. M is the midpoint of AB and X is on AB with AX : XB = 2 : 3. Find OM and OX.
steps: OM = a + ½(b - a) = ½(a + b)
AX = 2/5 AB so OX = a + 2/5 (b - a)
model.answer: OM = ½(a + b); OX = 3/5 a + 2/5 b

teach.note: Use 2/5 because the line is split into 5 equal parts, 2 of which are on A's side. Check the coefficients sum to 1 for a point on AB.

teach.heading: Hinge: ratio

check.q: P is on AB with AP : PB = 1 : 3. AP is:
check.why: There are 4 parts and AP is 1 of them: 1/4 AB. 1/3 compares AP to PB, not to the whole.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for BP in terms of AB (-3/4 AB).

teach.heading: Midpoint theorem

model.problem: In triangle OAB with OA = a and OB = b, M is the midpoint of OA and N is the midpoint of OB. Prove MN is parallel to AB and half its length.
steps: MN = ON - OM = ½b - ½a = ½(b - a)
So MN = ½ AB: parallel and half as long
model.answer: MN is parallel to AB and half its length

teach.note: Two vectors that are scalar multiples are parallel. Ask pupils for the geometric meaning: the line joining two midpoints is parallel to the third side.

teach.heading: Parallelogram diagonals

model.problem: OABC is a parallelogram with OA = a and OC = c. Prove the diagonals bisect each other.
steps: OB = a + c and AC = c - a
Midpoint of AC: a + ½(c - a) = ½(a + c)
Same point, so the diagonals bisect each other

teach.note: Both midpoints reach the same position vector, which proves they meet at that point. ANSWERS: practice: OM = ½(a + b); OX = 3/5 a + 2/5 b; MN = ½(b - a) = ½ AB; midpoints equal. exit: BA = a - b; show one is a scalar multiple of the other. core: OP = ⅓b so AP = ⅓b - a; midpoint of AP: a + ½(⅓b - a) = ½a + ⅙b; PQ = ½(a + b) - ⅓b = ½a + ⅙b. extend: PQ = ⅔(b - a) = ⅔AB so parallel. stretch: PQ = ½AC = SR (midpoint theorem in triangles ABC and ADC) so PQRS is a parallelogram. homework: written explanation.

practice: OA = a, OB = b. M is the midpoint of AB. Find OM in terms of a and b.
X divides AB so AX : XB = 2 : 3. Find OX.
In triangle OAB, M and N are midpoints of OA and OB. Show that MN is parallel to AB.
OABC is a parallelogram with OA = a and OC = c. Show that the diagonals bisect each other.
independent: Core: a) OA = a, OB = b. P is on OB with OP : PB = 1 : 2. Find AP and the midpoint of AP. b) Q is the midpoint of AB: find PQ.
Extend: In triangle OAB, P is on OA with OP = 2/3 OA and Q is on OB with OQ = 2/3 OB. Show PQ is parallel to AB.
Stretch: ABCD is a quadrilateral. P, Q, R, S are midpoints of AB, BC, CD, DA. Prove PQRS is a parallelogram.
exit: Write BA in terms of a and b when OA = a and OB = b.
How can vectors show two lines are parallel?
Big question: Can vectors prove things about shapes without a diagram?
lessons.homework: Explain in words how a vector proof differs from a proof using angles.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a fully labelled diagram and a route table for each vector; prompt the 'go via O' strategy. EAL: 'collinear', 'parallel', 'midpoint'. Stretch: show three points are collinear using vector multiples. Higher-only: vector geometric arguments and proofs (G25).

lessons.unit: S1-S6: Statistics
lessons.title: Populations, samples and sampling methods
lessons.bigQuestion: Can a small group tell us the truth about a whole population?
objectives: Distinguish a population from a sample
Describe random, systematic and stratified sampling
Use a sample to estimate a population, including capture-recapture
successCriteria: All: explain why a sample can be biased and how to reduce bias
Most: choose and carry out stratified sampling
Some: estimate a population from a sample, including capture-recapture
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography and biology: fieldwork sampling
lessons.smsc: Justice ('adl) and fairness: a fair survey represents everyone, not just the people it is easy to ask.

keywords.def: the whole group being studied
a smaller group selected from the population
an unfair preference that makes a sample unrepresentative

teach.heading: Sampling vocabulary
bullets: Population: everyone or everything we want to know about
Sample: the part we actually measure
Random: every member has an equal chance
Bias: some members are more likely to be chosen
teach.note: Ask for a population in the pupils' world (all pupils in the school) and a poor sample (only the football team). Connect to the idea of fairness in the smsc line.

teach.heading: Sampling methods

head: Method
How it works
Strength
Weakness
rows: Every member has an equal chance (numbers from a list or hat)
Choose every kth member after a random start
Sample each group in proportion to its size

teach.note: Pupils copy the table and then explain which method they would use for a survey on school meals. Higher: stratified sampling must be carried out with proportional calculation.
bullets: Larger samples reduce chance variation

teach.heading: Stratified sample

model.problem: A school has 600 pupils: Year 7 140, Year 8 120, Year 9 130, Year 10 110, Year 11 100. A stratified sample of 60 is needed. How many from each year?

teach.note: The numbers divide neatly here; in general round and check the total. Within each year, choose the pupils at random.

teach.heading: Capture-recapture

model.problem: A biologist catches 60 fish in a lake, marks them and releases them. Later she catches 50 fish and 8 are marked. Estimate the population of the lake.
steps: Fraction marked in the second sample = 8/50
Assume this equals the fraction in the whole lake: 60 ÷ N

teach.note: Higher only. Assumptions: the marked fish have mixed with the others, no fish enter, leave, die or lose marks. The formula is N = (marked first × second sample) ÷ marked in second.

teach.heading: Hinge: bias

check.q: Which sample is most likely to be biased when finding the healthiest foods people eat?
options: 100 people chosen randomly from the electoral register
100 people leaving a health food shop
100 people chosen at random from several towns
A stratified sample by age and area
check.why: People leaving a health food shop are more likely to eat healthily, so the sample is not representative.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask how to improve it (random sample from the whole population). ANSWERS: practice: 14, 12, 13, 11, 10; 40 × 60 ÷ 5 = 480; 24/80 × 600 = 180; biased by time and place, and only commuters. exit: bigger samples reduce chance variation; it often over-represents some people. core: take every 20th name after a random start between 1 and 20; stratified gives every year its fair share; N = 50 × 40 ÷ 4 = 500, assuming the marked fish mixed fully and the population did not change; extend: self-selected, small, possibly biased by incentive. homework: pupils' design.

practice: A school has 600 pupils (Y7 140, Y8 120, Y9 130, Y10 110, Y11 100). Find a stratified sample of 60.
40 fish are marked and released. A sample of 60 contains 5 marked. Estimate the population.
A random sample of 80 pupils finds that 24 walk to school. Estimate the number of walkers among 600 pupils.
A survey is carried out only at 8 am outside a train station. Give two reasons for bias.
independent: Core: a) Explain how to select a systematic sample of 30 from 600 pupils on a list. b) Compare stratified and simple random sampling for the survey of 600 pupils.
Extend: A lake survey: 50 marked and released; second sample of 40 contains 4 marked. Estimate the number, and say what assumption you made. Why might the estimate be too high or too low?
Stretch: A company claims that '90% of customers are happy' after surveying 20 people who left reviews. Give three criticisms.
exit: Why is a sample of 1000 better than a sample of 10?
State one disadvantage of convenience sampling.
Big question: Can a small group tell us the truth about a whole population?
lessons.homework: Design a fair survey to find out how Year 10 pupils get to school. State the population, the method and the sample size.
lessons.send: SEND: give the sampling fraction as a fraction line and a table to fill; use physical names in a hat. EAL: 'population', 'sample', 'bias'. Stretch: criticise real-world survey claims. Higher-only: stratified sampling calculations and capture-recapture.

lessons.unit: S1-S6: Statistics
lessons.title: Tables, charts and time series
lessons.bigQuestion: Which chart tells the truest story?
objectives: Draw and interpret pie charts and stem-and-leaf diagrams
Interpret bar charts and time series, including trend and seasonality
Spot misleading graphs
successCriteria: All: calculate pie chart angles and read a stem-and-leaf diagram
Most: describe the trend and seasonal pattern of a time series
Some: identify misleading scales and give a fair conclusion
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography and PSHE: reading data in the news
lessons.smsc: Honesty (sidq): presenting data so that it is not misleading.

keywords.def: a circle divided into sectors in proportion to frequencies
data recorded at regular times
the general direction of the data over time

teach.heading: Pie chart

model.problem: 120 pupils travel to school: 45 walk, 30 take the bus, 25 come by car, 20 cycle. Find the pie chart angles.

teach.note: Show the 'angle per person' step. Read: a sector of 90° is a quarter of the pupils, so 30.

teach.heading: Stem-and-leaf

model.problem: Draw an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram for 23, 25, 31, 34, 34, 38, 42, 45, 47, 51, 53, 58. Find the median and range.
steps: 12 values: median is between the 6th (38) and 7th (42): 40

teach.note: The key is essential. The diagram shows the shape of the data and keeps every value. Back-to-back diagrams compare two sets.

teach.heading: A time series: kilograms of dates sold
teach.note: Describe two features: an upward trend (each year higher than the last) and a seasonal pattern (Q4 is the highest each year, Q2 the lowest). Predict: Year 4 Q4 might be about 270, but this is an extrapolation and uncertain.
bullets: Trend plus seasonal pattern

teach.heading: Hinge: pie chart

check.q: 300 people: 75 chose tea. The pie chart angle for tea is:
check.why: 75 ÷ 300 = 1/4, and 1/4 of 360° = 90°. 75° uses the frequency as the angle; 25° is the percentage.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for the angle per person (1.2°).

teach.heading: Misleading scales

misconception.wrong: A bar chart showing sales of 50 and 55 looks as if sales have doubled.
misconception.right: Check the vertical axis: starting at 48 not 0 exaggerates a 10% rise.

teach.note: Show the same chart with a zero baseline. Ask pupils to find three ways a graph can mislead: truncated axis, uneven scale, 3D effects. ANSWERS: practice: 135°, 90°, 75°, 60°; median 40; upward trend with a Q4 peak each year; 90°. exit: 80°; trend or seasonality. core: French 144°, Spanish 120°, Arabic 96°; medians compared with a conclusion. extend: check the axis starts at zero, scales are even and the time period is representative. stretch: trend is the general direction; seasonality is a repeating pattern linked to the season. homework: pupil work.

practice: 120 pupils: walk 45, bus 30, car 25, cycle 20. Find the pie chart angles.
Draw a stem-and-leaf for 23, 25, 31, 34, 34, 38, 42, 45, 47, 51, 53, 58 and find the median.
Use the dates table to describe the trend and the seasonal pattern.
300 people: 75 chose tea. Find the angle for tea.
independent: Core: a) 90 pupils choose a language: French 36, Spanish 30, Arabic 24. Pie chart angles. b) Draw a back-to-back stem-and-leaf for two sets (give your own two lists of 8 numbers) and compare medians.
Extend: A newspaper graph shows crime falling steeply. Describe what to check on the graph.
Stretch: The time series of monthly rainfall for a town: describe what trend and seasonality mean and what may cause them.
exit: Find the pie chart angle for 20 pupils out of 90.
Write down a feature of a time series.
Big question: Which chart tells the truest story?
lessons.homework: Find a chart from a newspaper or website and comment in four sentences on whether it is fair or misleading.
lessons.send: SEND: give angle per item as a fraction line and protractor guides. EAL: 'trend', 'seasonal', 'key'. Stretch: draw a frequency polygon from grouped data.

lessons.unit: S1-S6: Statistics
lessons.title: Histograms with unequal class widths
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do we plot frequency density instead of frequency?
objectives: Calculate frequency density
Draw a histogram with unequal class widths
Read frequencies and estimate values from a histogram
successCriteria: All: calculate frequency density and frequency
Most: draw and read a histogram with unequal classes
Some: estimate a median or a number in a range from a histogram
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography and Biology: grouped data such as heights
lessons.smsc: Fair comparison: area must stand for amount, not height alone.

keywords.def: frequency ÷ class width
the size of a class interval
a chart where the area of each bar represents the frequency

starter: Find the class width of 10 < t ≤ 30.

teach.heading: From a table to a histogram
teach.note: Higher only. Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width. The area of each bar equals the frequency. The 160 < h ≤ 180 bar is wide so its height is lower than 30.
bullets: Area of bar = frequency

teach.heading: Reading a histogram

model.problem: A histogram has bars: 0-10 with density 1.6, 10-30 with density 2.4, 30-40 with density 3.0 and 40-60 with density 0.9. Find each frequency, the total and the median.
steps: Median is the 56th value: cumulative 16 then 64, so it lies in 10-30

teach.note: Interpolation assumes the data are spread evenly in the class. The number in the 20-35 range would be 10 × 2.4 + 5 × 3.0 = 39.

teach.heading: Hinge: frequency

check.q: A bar has width 5 and frequency density 4. The frequency is:
check.why: Frequency = frequency density × class width = 20. 9 adds them; 0.8 divides.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask which bar would be wider if the frequency were the same but the class twice as wide.

teach.heading: Estimating a number

model.problem: Using the heights table, estimate how many people have height between 165 cm and 180 cm.
steps: 165-180 is part of the class 160-180 with density 1.5

teach.note: Assumes even spread within the class. Compare with fractions of the class: 15/20 of 30 = 22.5.

teach.heading: Height equals frequency

misconception.wrong: The 160-180 bar is tallest since it has the most people, 30.
misconception.right: Height shows frequency density: 1.5, lower than the 150-160 bar (2.0), because the class is wider.

teach.note: Always ask 'what is on the vertical axis?' and use area. ANSWERS: practice: 0.8, 2.0, 1.5, 0.3; frequencies 16, 48, 30, 18; 22.5; area must represent frequency since classes differ in width. exit: 0.9; the class width changes so the height measures density. core: densities 1.5, 3.6, 1.5, 0.3; between 25 and 40: 15 × 1.5 = 22.5; modal class 10-20 (highest density). extend: total 93, median is the 46.5th: 15 + 36 = 51 at 20 so it lies in 10-20: 10 + (46.5 - 15) ÷ 36 × 10 = 18.75. stretch: 18 and 18, so the remaining total is 56 - 36 = 20. homework: histogram drawn.

practice: Complete the density column: 8, 20, 30, 6 for classes of width 10, 10, 20, 20.
From density 1.6, 2.4, 3.0 and 0.9 with widths 10, 20, 10, 20 find the frequencies.
Estimate the number in 165-180 cm.
State why a histogram needs frequency density.
independent: Core: a) Quiz times: 0 < t ≤ 10: 15; 10 < t ≤ 20: 36; 20 < t ≤ 40: 30; 40 < t ≤ 80: 12. Find the frequency densities and the number between 25 and 40 minutes. b) State the modal class.
Extend: Estimate the median time for the quiz.
Stretch: A histogram has the bar 20-30 with height 1.8 and 30-50 with height 0.9 and total frequency 56. Find the frequencies in these bars and the remaining total.
exit: Find the frequency density of a class 40 < t ≤ 60 with frequency 18.
Explain why bar height is not the frequency when the classes are unequal.
Big question: Why do we plot frequency density instead of frequency?
lessons.homework: Draw a histogram of the quiz times data on graph paper with a labelled density axis.
lessons.send: SEND: use a calculation table with columns for width, frequency and density; use squared paper. EAL: 'density', 'width', 'frequency'. Stretch: reconstruct the table from a drawn histogram with a given scale. Higher-only: this whole lesson (S3).

lessons.unit: S1-S6: Statistics
lessons.title: Cumulative frequency, quartiles and box plots
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a single graph show the middle and the spread of a large data set?
objectives: Draw a cumulative frequency graph
Estimate the median, quartiles and interquartile range
Draw and interpret box plots
successCriteria: All: draw a cumulative frequency graph with correct plotting points
Most: read the median and quartiles from the graph
Some: draw a box plot and compare two distributions
lessons.crossCurricular: Science and PE: comparing performance data
lessons.smsc: Fair comparison of different groups: use the same measures for both.

keywords.def: a running total of frequencies
upper quartile minus lower quartile
a diagram showing the minimum, quartiles, median and maximum

teach.heading: Cumulative frequency table: test marks of 80 pupils
teach.note: Higher only. Plot each cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary: (10, 4), (20, 14), (30, 36), (40, 62), (50, 76), (60, 80), starting at (0, 0). Join with a smooth curve.
bullets: Plot against the upper boundary

teach.heading: Reading the graph

model.problem: For the 80 marks, estimate the median, lower quartile, upper quartile and interquartile range.
steps: Median at cumulative frequency 40: between 36 (at 30) and 62 (at 40): 30 + 4/26 × 10 ≈ 31.5

teach.note: Read from the graph in an exam: draw lines at 40, 20 and 60 across to the curve and down. Accept a range of values; show the lines. For n values, use n/2, n/4 and 3n/4.

teach.heading: Hinge: quartile position

check.q: In a cumulative frequency graph for 80 values the lower quartile is read at a cumulative frequency of:
check.why: Lower quartile is at 1/4 of the data: 80 ÷ 4 = 20. 40 is the median; 60 the upper quartile.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for the upper quartile position (60).

teach.heading: Box plot summary
teach.note: Draw the box from the LQ to the UQ with a line at the median and whiskers to the lowest and highest values. Ask what the box represents (middle 50% of the data) and why the IQR ignores outliers.
bullets: Box = middle 50%

teach.heading: Comparing

model.problem: Another class has median 36 and IQR 9. Compare with this class (median 31.5, IQR 16.5).
steps: Median: the second class is higher (36 against 31.5) so typically scored more
IQR: the second class is smaller (9 against 16.5) so the marks are more consistent
Conclusion: the second class did better and more consistently
model.answer: Second class higher and more consistent

teach.note: Always give one comment on average and one on spread, with numbers, in context. ANSWERS: practice: 4, 14, 36, 62, 76, 80; median ≈ 31.5, LQ ≈ 22.7, UQ ≈ 39.2, IQR ≈ 16.5; box plot from 3 to 58; second class is higher and more consistent. exit: 60 and 90; the spread of the middle 50% of the data. core: more than 45: 80 - cumulative at 45 (about 69) so about 11; 90th percentile at cumulative frequency 72: 40 + (72 - 62)/14 × 10 ≈ 47.1. extend: IQR = 9; upper fence = 24 + 13.5 = 37.5 so 40 is an outlier. stretch: X has a larger spread (IQR 20 against 11) and a lower middle; Y is more consistent with a higher median. homework: pupil sentences.

practice: Complete the cumulative frequency column for the marks table.
Estimate the median, LQ, UQ and IQR from the graph.
Draw the box plot for the marks.
A second class has median 36 and IQR 9. Compare.
independent: Core: a) Use the graph to estimate how many pupils scored more than 45. b) Estimate the 90th percentile.
Extend: A set of times has min 12, LQ 15, median 18, UQ 24 and max 40. Draw the box plot and find the IQR. State whether 40 is an outlier by the rule UQ + 1.5 × IQR.
Stretch: Compare two box plots: Class X: 20, 35, 42, 55, 80; Class Y: 30, 38, 43, 49, 60 (min, LQ, median, UQ, max).
exit: For 120 values, state the cumulative frequency at which the median and upper quartile are read.
What does the interquartile range measure?
Big question: How can a single graph show the middle and the spread of a large data set?
lessons.homework: Write three comparison sentences for two box plots of your own choice: one about average, one about spread, one about the overall conclusion.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a pre-labelled grid and a table with the plotting points; use rulers for reading. EAL: 'cumulative', 'quartile', 'median'. Stretch: outliers and the 1.5 × IQR rule. Higher-only: cumulative frequency, quartiles, IQR and box plots (S3, S4).

lessons.unit: S1-S6: Statistics
lessons.title: Comparing distributions: averages, spread and populations
lessons.bigQuestion: Which average, and which measure of spread, tells the fairest story?
objectives: Estimate the mean from a grouped frequency table
Choose the best average for a situation
Compare distributions using averages and spread and use statistics to describe a population
successCriteria: All: calculate the mean, median and mode from tables
Most: choose a suitable average and measure of spread
Some: compare two distributions in context and combine means
lessons.crossCurricular: Economics and PE: averages in the real world
lessons.smsc: Truthful reporting: the choice of average should not mislead.

keywords.def: the mean found using midpoints of class intervals
a value that is much larger or smaller than the others
how far the data are from the middle

teach.heading: Mean from a grouped table

model.problem: Use the marks table: classes 0-10: 4, 10-20: 10, 20-30: 22, 30-40: 26, 40-50: 14, 50-60: 4. Estimate the mean and give the modal class and median class.
model.answer: Estimated mean 31.0; modal and median class 30-40

teach.note: It is an estimate because we do not know the exact values. Use the midpoint as a representative value.

teach.heading: The best average

model.problem: Five workers earn £22 000, £24 000, £25 000, £26 000 and £150 000. Find the mean and the median, and say which is more representative.
steps: The £150 000 is an outlier pulling the mean up

teach.note: Mean: uses all the values but is affected by extremes. Median: unaffected by outliers. Mode: useful for categorical data or the most common value.

teach.heading: Hinge: the average

check.q: A data set has an extreme outlier. The best average to use is:
check.why: The median is not affected by one extreme value. The range is a measure of spread, not an average.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask which measure of spread is best here (IQR).

teach.heading: Comparing two groups

model.problem: Boys' 100 m times: median 14.2 s, IQR 1.5 s. Girls' times: median 13.8 s, IQR 2.4 s. Compare.
steps: Girls have the lower median so are typically faster
Girls have the higher IQR so are less consistent
Conclusion: girls were faster on average but with more variation
model.answer: Girls faster on average but less consistent

teach.note: Two comments with numbers and context. Use 'typically' and 'on average', not 'all girls'.

teach.heading: Combined mean

model.problem: A class of 20 has mean 62 and a class of 30 has mean 70. Find the mean of all 50.

teach.note: The combined mean is between 62 and 70 and nearer the larger class. It is not (62 + 70) ÷ 2. ANSWERS: practice: 31.0; mean £49 400, median £25 000, so median; girls faster on average but less consistent; 66.8. exit: 5; (10 + 75 + 75) ÷ 10 = 16. core: (a) midpoints 2.5, 7.5, 15: (15 + 105 + 300) ÷ 40 = 10.5; (b) a few high earners raise the mean so it is not typical. extend: the sample mean estimates the population mean, but it varies from sample to sample and depends on random sampling. stretch: the same average but the second set is less consistent. homework: pupil work.

practice: Five workers earn £22 000, £24 000, £25 000, £26 000, £150 000. Find mean and median and choose.
Boys' median 14.2, IQR 1.5; girls' median 13.8, IQR 2.4: compare.
A class of 20 has mean 62 and a class of 30 has mean 70. Find the combined mean.
independent: Core: a) Estimate the mean from: 0-5: 6, 5-10: 14, 10-20: 20. b) A shop reports 'the average wage is £30 000'. Explain how this could mislead.
Extend: A sample of 100 households gives a mean household size of 3.4. Explain how to use this to describe the population, and one limitation.
Stretch: Two data sets have the same mean but different IQRs. Interpret.
exit: Find the mode of 3, 5, 5, 6, 8.
Estimate the mean from a grouped table when the class midpoints are 5, 15, 25 and frequencies 2, 5, 3.
Big question: Which average, and which measure of spread, tells the fairest story?
lessons.homework: Pick two sets of data from the internet (e.g. temperatures of two cities) and compare them using a median and a measure of spread.
lessons.send: SEND: use a table with columns for midpoint and f × midpoint; use a calculator. EAL: 'average', 'spread', 'consistent'. Stretch: weighted means and combined groups. Higher-only: comparing using IQR and combined means; Foundation: mean, median, mode and range.

lessons.unit: S1-S6: Statistics
lessons.title: Scatter graphs, correlation and lines of best fit
lessons.bigQuestion: If two things move together, does one cause the other?
objectives: Plot and describe scatter graphs
Draw a line of best fit and use it to estimate
Identify correlation, outliers and the danger of extrapolation
successCriteria: All: describe the type of correlation
Most: draw a line of best fit and make an estimate
Some: explain the difference between correlation and causation and the limits of extrapolation
lessons.crossCurricular: Science and PE: relationships between variables
lessons.smsc: Care in claiming: we do not assert more than the data show.

keywords.def: a relationship between two variables
a straight line drawn through the middle of the points
using the line outside the range of the data

starter: Find the gradient of the line through (1, 35) and (8, 80).
Find y when x = 5.5 in y = 6.2x + 29.

teach.heading: Hours of revision and test score
teach.note: Pupils plot the eight points. They show strong positive correlation. The mean point is (4.5, 57.25). A line of best fit through the mean point has gradient about 6.2 so y ≈ 6.2x + 29.
bullets: Positive: both increase together

teach.heading: Using the line

model.problem: Use the line y ≈ 6.2x + 29. Estimate the score for 5.5 hours, and the score for 15 hours. Comment on each.
steps: x = 5.5: y ≈ 6.2 × 5.5 + 29 = 63 (interpolation, within the data range)
122 is impossible if the test has a maximum of 100
Interpolation is reliable; extrapolation may not be

teach.note: The line is a model for the range of the data. Beyond it the relationship may not hold. Accept answers in a range from the pupils' own lines, for example 62 to 65.

teach.heading: Hinge: correlation

check.q: A scatter graph shows strong negative correlation. This means:
options: as x increases, y decreases, with the points close to a line
check.why: Negative: one goes up as the other goes down; strong: points close to the line. A causal claim needs more evidence.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for an example of negative correlation: the age of a car and its value.

teach.heading: Correlation is not causation

misconception.wrong: Ice cream sales and sunburn cases are correlated, so ice cream causes sunburn.
misconception.right: Both increase because of a third factor: hot sunny weather.

teach.note: Ask for another example. In an exam say 'correlation does not mean causation'; suggest a lurking variable.

teach.heading: Line of best fit rules

model.problem: A car's value (£1000s) against age: (1, 14), (2, 12.5), (3, 11), (5, 8), (6, 7), (8, 4.5). Describe the correlation and estimate the value at 4 years.
steps: Line of best fit: about y = -1.36x + 15.2

teach.note: Drawing rules: pass through the mean point, roughly equal points above and below, ignore outliers. Extrapolate to 12 years gives -1.1: impossible, so extrapolation is unreliable. ANSWERS: practice: strong positive correlation; about 63 (accept 62 to 65); 15 hours is outside the range and gives a score above 100; ice cream sales and sunburn. exit: negative correlation; interpolation is within the range of the data and extrapolation is outside it. core: strong negative; about £9800; at 12 years the line gives about -£1100 which is impossible; the outlier is a special case that should be ignored when drawing the line but mentioned. extend: both depend on age or growth; correlation is not causation. stretch: gradient about -1.36 means the car loses about £1360 in value each year. homework: pupil data.

practice: Plot the eight points of hours against score, describe the correlation and draw a line of best fit.
Use your line to estimate the score for 5.5 hours.
Why is using the line to predict the score for 15 hours unreliable?
Give an example of two variables with correlation but no causation.
independent: Core: a) Plot the car value data and draw a line of best fit. b) Estimate the value at 4 years and comment on the value at 12 years. c) One car is a classic, age 7, value £25 000: what is this point called and what do you do with it?
Extend: A scatter graph of shoe size against height shows positive correlation. Explain whether bigger feet cause greater height.
Stretch: Find the equation of your line of best fit from two points on it, and interpret the gradient in context.
exit: State the type of correlation between age of a car and its value.
Explain the difference between interpolation and extrapolation.
Big question: If two things move together, does one cause the other?
lessons.homework: Collect data from your family or friends (e.g. height and arm span) for 8 people. Plot a scatter graph, describe the correlation and draw a line of best fit.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a pre-drawn grid and a printed table; use a ruler and a clear plotting instruction. EAL: 'correlation', 'outlier', 'extrapolate'. Stretch: use the mean point to build the equation of a line of best fit.
